title: What would happen if the speed of light were only one mile per hour?
text: If the speed of light were only as fast as a slow walk—one mile per hour—then everything in the universe would feel like it was moving through thick syrup. You could easily outrun light on a bike, and you'd see weird things like the sun suddenly going dark if you turned your head away, because the light from it would take over a week to reach Earth instead of just eight minutes. Even simple actions like flipping a light switch would mean waiting for the light to slowly creep across the room, and things like GPS and cell phones wouldn't work at all because the signals would be too slow. Basically, our whole understanding of time and space would get tangled up, making the world a very strange and sluggish place.

title: Why can't humans taste water?
text: Humans can taste water, but it's not like tasting something sweet or sour because water doesn't have a strong flavor of its own—instead, our tongues notice water by how it changes the taste of other things, like washing away salty or sugary tastes, which helps our bodies know when we're drinking and stay hydrated.

title: What is the neuroscience of meditation/spirituality?
text: Think of your brain like a busy city with lots of cars (your thoughts) zooming around on roads. When you meditate or do something spiritual like praying quietly, it’s like you’re telling most of the cars to pull over and stop for a little while. This lets the city calm down. Your brain actually changes: the part that worries (like an alarm bell) gets quieter, and the part that helps you pay attention and feel calm gets stronger, almost like exercising a muscle. It can also help you feel more connected to others, like realizing all the separate cars are part of one big city.

title: How do different eyesight problems differ to each other? i.e. long sighted, short sighted, astigmatism
text: Think of your eye like a camera that needs to focus a picture perfectly on the back wall. If the picture is blurry, something about the camera's shape is a little off. Being nearsighted (short-sighted) means your eye is a bit too long, so the picture focuses in front of the back wall, making far-away things blurry but close-up things clear. Being farsighted (long-sighted) is the opposite—your eye is a bit too short, so the picture tries to focus behind the back wall, making close things blurry while far things can be clearer. Astigmatism is different—it’s like your eye is shaped more like a football instead of a basketball, so the light gets bent unevenly and makes everything look a little blurry or stretched out, both up close and far away.

title: Where do we get the chemicals used in laboratories to create medicine?
text: We get the chemicals for medicine from many places, like plants, animals, and even rocks, but most are now made in factories by mixing simpler ingredients together, kind of like following a recipe to bake a cake.

title: How does a police officer prove his radar reading was specifically for your car when there's hundreds of cars whizzing by on a busy highway?
text: A police officer's radar gun is like a super-focused flashlight that only shines on one car at a time—it picks the biggest and closest target, so when the officer points it at your car and pulls the trigger, it's measuring your speed and not the others around you.

title: What makes it possible to control a touch screen while lightly hovering your finger over the screen?
text: Some touch screens can feel your finger before you even touch them because they use a special kind of electricity called capacitance—imagine the screen has a tiny, invisible blanket of electricity spread over it. When your finger gets close, it interrupts that blanket like a rock making ripples in a pond, and the screen senses exactly where that happened so it knows where you’re pointing.

title: What's actually making those ticking noises when your car cools down after being shut off?
text: When your car cools down after you turn it off, the ticking noises you hear are usually the metal parts in the engine and exhaust system shrinking as they get cooler—imagine a metal toy left in the sun that gets bigger when hot and then makes little clicks as it cools and gets smaller again, because all the parts don’t cool at exactly the same speed.

title: What is the argument against a flat tax in the US?
text: Imagine everyone has a different amount of candy. A flat tax is like saying everyone must give the same *number* of candies, like 2 candies each. For a kid with only 5 candies, losing 2 is a big deal and leaves them with very little. But for a kid with 100 candies, losing 2 is easy and they still have a huge pile. The argument against a flat tax is that it's not fair to take the same amount from everyone because it hurts poor people a lot more than rich people, and many people think taxes should be based on how much candy you actually have.

title: why do so many people film cellphone videos in portrait mode?
text: People film in portrait mode because it feels natural to hold a phone up and down like they're taking a picture, and it's perfect for faces and things close up, but it's not as good for wide scenes like a soccer game because you miss what's happening on the sides.

title: why do you get a bruise when something is "suctioned" onto you?
text: When you get a bruise from something like a suction cup, it's because the strong pull creates a tiny vacuum that tugs so hard on your skin and the little blood vessels underneath that some of them break, letting blood leak out under your skin and making that familiar purple mark.

title: Could a very steamy shower and closed door cause a person to asphyxiate from too much steam and too little oxygen (being pushed aside by the steam)?
text: No, you can't suffocate from a steamy shower because steam is just tiny water droplets and doesn't push away enough oxygen—you'd get too hot and uncomfortable and leave the bathroom long before you ran out of air to breathe.

title: What is the immediate protocol for if a U.S. president tries to sieze absolute power?
text: If a U.S. president tried to grab all the power for themselves, it would be like a player in a game trying to break all the rules and be the only one who gets to decide everything. The good news is that the people who made the rules a long time ago thought this might happen, so they built lots of stops into the game. First, other leaders in the government, like Congress and the courts, would say "no, you can't do that" and would use their own powers to stop any illegal orders. The military and police leaders are sworn to follow the Constitution's rules, not just the president, so they would also refuse to carry out illegal commands. If the president kept trying, Congress could quickly impeach them and remove them from their job. It's designed so that no single person, not even the president, can take over because many, many other people have a piece of the power and a duty to protect the rules.

title: What powers do the "One Ring" and the Rings of Power give ?
text: The One Ring and the other Rings of Power are like special magic rings that give their wearers abilities based on who they are. The three rings for the elves mostly let them protect beautiful places, heal hurts, and keep things from fading or wearing out over time. The seven rings for the dwarves made them greedier for treasure and helped them build greater mines, but didn't control their minds. The nine rings for men gave them long life and power, but slowly turned them into invisible ghost-servants called Ringwraiths. The One Ring, made secretly by the dark lord Sauron, is the master ring—it can make the wearer invisible, gives long life, and can control the other rings, but its main power is to dominate the wills of all people and let Sauron rule the world.

title: How was it decided that clocks move "clockwise"?
text: Long ago, before clocks were invented, people used sundials to tell time, and in the northern part of the world, the shadow on a sundial moves in the direction we now call "clockwise" as the sun crosses the sky. When mechanical clocks were later created, the makers copied that familiar motion for the clock hands, and since most early clockmakers lived in the north, that direction just stuck for everyone.

title: Why are darker colors "dominant" genes whereas lighter colors are "recessive"?
text: Think of genes like tiny recipes for making colors, and you get one recipe from each parent—darker colors are like strong, bold instructions that are easy to follow, while lighter colors are like quiet, gentle instructions that get covered up if a bold one is around.

title: How do night contacts work?
text: Night contacts are special glasses you wear while you sleep that gently press on your eyes to temporarily change their shape, so when you wake up and take them out, you can see clearly all day without needing regular glasses or contacts.

title: Other than admission fee and parking, how do zoos make money?
text: Zoos make money by having gift shops where you can buy stuffed animals and toys, selling food like popcorn and ice cream at snack stands, and offering special experiences such as feeding a giraffe or having a birthday party on the grounds.

title: Math: In Poker, when trying to evaluate how likely it is that you will make the best hand by the river, it's assumed that the cards that'll make your winning hand are still in the deck, when they could have actually been dealt and folded already. Why is this?
text: When we figure out your chances in poker, we pretend all the cards you need are still in the deck because we don’t know where any of the folded cards went—it’s like they’re hiding in a big, messy pile we can’t see. Since we can’t peek at those hidden cards, the easiest and fairest guess is to act like the cards you want are still available to be dealt, just like guessing there’s still a piece of your favorite candy left in a mixed-up bag even though some pieces are already gone.

title: How does coffee work?
text: Coffee works by waking up your brain with a tiny helper called caffeine, which is like a pretend shout that tells your brain to stop feeling sleepy and pay attention.

title: Is it possible for a nuclear bomb to ignite the atmosphere on fire? If not, why did physicists think it was possible? If so, how?
text: No, it's not possible for a nuclear bomb to ignite the atmosphere on fire, but some physicists did briefly worry about it during the first atomic bomb test. They were concerned that the bomb's extreme heat might cause the nitrogen in the air to start fusing together like the sun does, which would spread and burn up the whole planet. They quickly did the math and realized our atmosphere is too thin and stable for that to happen—it's like how a match can light a dry leaf on fire but can't make a whole wet forest burn. So, while the bomb is incredibly powerful, it's nowhere near powerful enough to set the entire sky on fire.

title: How does Google manage to parse every page on it's database and show our search results on them in miliseconds?
text: Imagine Google has a giant library with copies of every single webpage, and before you even ask a question, it has already read all the books and made a super detailed card catalog that lists where every word appears—so when you search, it just checks its card catalog really fast to find exactly what you need.

title: How can siri or any other voice recognition software tell the difference when someone says your or you're, or its and it's?
text: Siri and other voice recognition software listen very carefully to the whole sentence you say, not just one word, and they use a big brain made of computer rules and examples to guess which word fits best—like knowing you say "you're happy" and "your toy" based on all the other words around it.

title: Why do some people grind their teeth at night?
text: Some people grind their teeth at night because their jaw gets really tight while they're sleeping, often because they feel stressed or worried during the day, and their mouth tries to chew on those feelings like it's chewing on a tough piece of gum.

title: Somalia has a GDP of around $6 Billion, Bill Gates has a net worth of roughly $86 Billion. What stops the mega wealthy from just moving to an impoverished country and literally buying it to become a monarch?
text: Even though it sounds like Bill Gates could buy Somalia because his money is bigger than their whole country's, it doesn't work like buying a toy or a house. A country isn't for sale—it's made of land, people, and laws that aren't owned by anyone. If a very rich person moved there, they couldn't just take over because the people and other countries wouldn't accept it, plus money is different from power; having a lot of cash doesn't mean you can tell everyone what to do or make them follow your rules.

title: Why are political views and parties called left/right wing?
text: Imagine you're in a big meeting a long time ago in France, where people who wanted big changes sat on the left side of the room, and people who wanted to keep things mostly the same sat on the right side. Over time, "left wing" came to mean ideas that usually focus on things like helping everyone share more equally and having the government play a big role in solving problems, while "right wing" came to mean ideas that usually focus on personal freedom, tradition, and having the government play a smaller role. It's just a simple way to group different kinds of ideas, like how we might call one group "team red" and another "team blue."

title: How/why are feelings of sadness and anger connected?
text: Imagine your feelings are like different colored paints in a box—sometimes they get mixed together. Sadness is like a blue paint, and anger is like a red paint. When something upsetting happens, you might first feel sad, like if a friend didn’t share a toy. But that sadness can feel big and scary, so your heart and brain might mix in some anger to help you feel stronger and protect yourself, like a shield. So, sadness and anger are connected because they often come from the same hurt place, and one can turn into the other to help you handle tough feelings.

title: What actually happens to the mobile phone networks/cell service when there is a large scale emergency or disaster? What do the networks do?
text: When lots of people try to use their phones at the same time during an emergency, it’s like a huge crowd trying to squeeze through a single door—everything gets stuck. Cell towers are like those doors, and they can only handle so many calls and texts at once. The networks know this might happen, so they try to help by giving emergency calls, like to 911, the very first spot in line so they can get through. Sometimes they can also add temporary, portable towers (like putting up an extra door) to busy areas. But if a tower gets broken by a storm or earthquake, then there’s just no service there until workers can go fix it.

title: How do We Remember?
text: Think of your brain like a big toy box with lots of drawers. When you learn something new, like a friend's name, your brain puts that memory into one of the drawers. To remember it later, your brain has to find the right drawer and open it. The more you play with that memory—like saying your friend's name over and over—the stronger and easier to find it becomes, just like your favorite toy that's always on top of the pile. If you don't use a memory much, it can get buried under other things, making it harder to find, but sometimes a clue (like seeing your friend's face) can help your brain dig it back up again.

title: Why are roof shingles so small?
text: Roof shingles are small because it's easier to fit them together like puzzle pieces to cover a bumpy or slanted roof, and if one gets damaged you can just replace that tiny piece instead of a huge sheet.

title: Why are smartphones getting thinner and thinner?
text: Smartphones are getting thinner because companies want them to be easier to carry in your pocket and more comfortable to hold, and they keep finding clever ways to squeeze all the important parts—like the battery and computer chips—into smaller, flatter spaces inside.

title: Why is it so much easier taking two steps at a time going up a stairwell, but so much more difficult (and scary) doing the same down a stairwell?
text: Going up stairs two at a time is easier because you’re using your strong leg muscles to push yourself up, and if you slip, you just fall back onto the step below, which isn’t too scary. Going down two at a time is harder and scarier because you have to control your weight while stepping down into empty space, and if you slip, you might tumble forward and fall a longer way, which could hurt a lot more.

title: When you rappel down a cliff, someone has to hold the rope at the bottom. How does the first person get down if this is so important?
text: The first person doesn't need someone at the bottom because they set up the rope at the top instead—they tie it to something very strong like a big rock or a special anchor, and then they can slide down the rope all by themselves.

title: How do we have "...94 million Americans out of the labor force"?
text: Think of the country like a big playground where everyone who is old enough can choose to play a game called "jobs." The "labor force" is the group of kids who are either playing the game right now or who are standing on the sidelines saying, "I want to play and I'm looking for a team to join." The "94 million out of the labor force" are all the other kids on the playground who are not playing that game and don't want to right now. This includes little kids who are too young, older kids who have retired and are just swinging on the swings, kids who are staying home to take care of their family, kids who are in school all day, and kids who are sick or can't play for other reasons. So it's not that 94 million people lost their jobs; it's that they are not even trying to play the jobs game at the moment.

title: When people smoke cigarettes, they put it between their pointer and middle fingers, but when people smoke joints, they use their thumbs and their index fingers. Why is this?
text: When people smoke cigarettes, they often hold them between their pointer and middle fingers because it's a comfortable and relaxed way to keep the cigarette away from their palm, which can get warm, and it looks cool in movies and pictures. But when people smoke joints, they usually pinch them between their thumb and index finger because joints are softer and can bend or go out if you hold them too loosely, so pinching helps keep them straight and burning evenly.

title: Why is it that men and women tend to take off their shirts differently?
text: Men and women often take off their shirts differently because of the clothes they usually wear—men’s shirts are often looser and can be pulled straight over the head, while women’s shirts can be tighter or have delicate features like buttons, so they might take them off more carefully by pulling from the bottom or unbuttoning first.

title: What's the difference between Apple Juice and Apple Cider?
text: Apple juice is made by squeezing apples and then filtering out all the pulp and cloudy bits, so it's clear and smooth. Apple cider is also made by squeezing apples, but it keeps all the pulp and bits in, so it looks cloudy and tastes stronger, like fresh apples.

title: when you are sick and you swallow and your ears crackle, what is actually happening in your ears?
text: When you're sick and your ears crackle, it's because the tube that connects your ear to the back of your nose gets a little clogged with mucus, and when you swallow, you're helping to open it up and move air through, which makes that crackling sound.

title: Why does Mexico get cane sugar Coca Cola while the U.S. gets high-fructose corn syrup Coke?
text: In the U.S., corn is grown a lot and made into a cheaper sweetener called high-fructose corn syrup, so Coca-Cola uses it to save money. In Mexico, sugar cane is easier to get and often costs less than that corn syrup, so they use real cane sugar instead, which some people think tastes a little different.

title: Why do we compare defence budgets between countries?
text: We compare defense budgets because it's like checking how much money different kids have saved up for their lemonade stand security—it gives us a clue about how strong and ready their "team" is, and helps everyone guess if they might get into a fight or work together as friends.

title: Why does old plastic go yellow? Will that happen to plastics made recently too?
text: Old plastic turns yellow because of a chemical reaction that happens when it's exposed to sunlight and air for a long time, kind of like how a banana peel turns brown. The light and oxygen slowly break down the plastic's ingredients, making it change color. This can still happen to newer plastics, but many are now made with special protectors mixed in to help them stay clear for much longer.

title: What would it take for us to be able to (assuming it's ever possible) create a spacecraft capable of going even half the speed of light? Also, is constant acceleration feasible in terms of space travel?
text: To go half the speed of light, we'd need a spaceship with a super powerful engine that doesn't use the heavy fuel rockets do today—instead, it might push itself with something like a nuclear explosion behind it or a giant sail pushed by lasers from Earth. The biggest problem is that space isn't completely empty; even tiny specks of dust would hit the ship like bullets at that speed, so we'd need a very strong shield. Constant acceleration, like always feeling a gentle push forward, would be great because you could get to faraway stars faster and even create artificial gravity inside the ship, but with our current engines we'd run out of fuel too quickly. To make constant acceleration work, we'd need an engine that can run for years without carrying all its fuel, like one that scoops hydrogen from space as it goes, but we don't know how to build that yet.

title: If you had a solid sphere with similar size and mass of the Earth and bored a hole from one end to the other through the center and dropped a penny into the hole, assuming the sphere's gravity is the only acting force, what would happen to the penny?
text: If you dropped a penny into a hole that goes straight through the center of an Earth-sized ball, the penny would fall faster and faster until it reached the very middle, then it would slow down as it kept going to the other side, almost like a roller coaster—it would pop out the other end and then fall back in again, going back and forth forever.

title: How does my key fob only work on my car?
text: Think of your key fob as a tiny walkie-talkie that only knows a secret password with your car. When you press the button, it shouts that special password, and your car is always listening for it. Since your car only knows its own secret password, it ignores all the other key fobs shouting at other cars, just like you would only answer if someone called your own name.

title: Why do fish swim relatively vertical?
text: Fish swim vertically because they have a special swim bladder inside them that works like a tiny balloon, helping them float at just the right depth without having to paddle all the time.

title: Why do women get their tubes tied when men get their vas deferens cut?
text: Women get their tubes tied and men get their vas deferens cut because both are ways to make it so a person can't have babies anymore, but they are done on different body parts. Women have fallopian tubes that carry eggs, and tying them blocks the path. Men have a tube called the vas deferens that carries sperm, and cutting it blocks the path. Doctors usually do the simpler surgery on men because it’s easier and safer, like a quick fix compared to a bigger project.

title: Whydo developers still use Unreal Engine 3 if Unreal Engine 4 is available?
text: Think of game engines like toy boxes. Unreal Engine 4 is a brand new, huge toy box with all the latest, fanciest toys that can build really big and shiny things, but it can be complicated to learn and some of the toys are so new that the instructions aren't perfect yet. Unreal Engine 3 is like your older, trusty toy box; you already know exactly how every toy inside works, it's easier to carry around, and it still has plenty of cool stuff to build exactly what you want. Sometimes a developer has a project that fits perfectly in that older toy box, and switching to the new one would mean starting all over, so they just keep using the one they know best.

title: What is the white powder that is on chewing gum for?
text: That white powder is like a special dust that keeps the gum from sticking to everything—imagine if you took two pieces of paper and put glue on them, they’d stick together, but if you sprinkled a little baby powder between them, they wouldn’t stick anymore. The gum starts out soft and sticky, so the powder keeps it from sticking to the wrapper or to other pieces of gum in the package.

title: What happens in our body at the exact time when we fall asleep? Where is the border between consciousness and unconsciousness?
text: Imagine your brain is like a busy playground during the day, with lots of kids (your thoughts and senses) running around and playing. When it's time to fall asleep, it's like a teacher slowly starts turning off the lights and asking the kids to quiet down. The exact moment you fall asleep is when the last few kids finally stop playing and sit down—your brain switches from being awake and aware to starting its sleep chores. The border between being awake and asleep is fuzzy, like drifting off during a boring movie; you don't notice the exact second it happens, but suddenly you're dreaming and your body is repairing itself and sorting memories.

title: Why do oysters create pearls and yet other shellfish don't?
text: Oysters create pearls as a way to protect themselves when something irritating, like a tiny grain of sand, gets inside their shell. They cover it with a smooth, shiny material called nacre, which is the same stuff that lines their shell, and over time that builds up into a pearl. Other shellfish, like clams or mussels, usually don’t make pearls because their bodies react differently to irritants—they might just push it out instead of coating it, or they don’t produce enough nacre to form a nice round pearl. So, while some other shellfish can occasionally make pearls, oysters are the best at it because they’re really good at layering that shiny material over and over.

title: Why does Walmart have fantastic prices in every department besides video gaming?
text: Walmart can offer low prices on most things because they buy huge amounts from companies, but video games are different because the companies that make them, like Nintendo or PlayStation, set the prices themselves and don’t allow big discounts so all stores charge about the same.

title: What is 'Legacy Code' in programming?
text: Legacy code is like an old toy that you still play with but nobody remembers exactly how it works anymore; it's a piece of software that was written a long time ago, often by people who aren't around now, and it can be tricky to update or fix because it uses old ideas or languages that newer programmers might not know well.

title: Why do pigeons and doves look the same all around the world? Also, why ARE they all around the world?
text: Pigeons and doves look similar everywhere because they all come from the same bird family a long time ago, like cousins who all have the same grandparents. They are found all over the world because they are very good at traveling and adapting; some kinds flew to new places on their own, while people brought others along because they are useful for food, as pets, or even for carrying messages, and once they arrived, they learned to live almost anywhere, eating whatever food they could find.

title: why do men feel tired/sleepy after orgasm or ejaculating?
text: Think of your body like a busy toy factory that's always making energy to play and run around, but after an orgasm, it sends out a special sleepy chemical called prolactin and turns down the "awake" chemicals for a little while, making you feel relaxed and ready for a nap, just like after a big, fun playtime.

title: Why is breathing pure oxygen toxic?
text: Breathing pure oxygen for too long is like eating only candy for every meal—it might seem great at first, but it can actually hurt your body because it’s just too much of a good thing. Your body is used to the air we normally breathe, which is mostly a gas called nitrogen with just a little bit of oxygen mixed in. When you breathe pure oxygen, it can irritate your lungs and, over time, cause damage because it’s so strong and reactive. It’s a bit like how too much sunshine gives you a sunburn instead of a nice warm feeling.

title: Why is physical attraction so important when finding a partner?
text: Imagine you're picking out a toy to play with—you're naturally drawn to the one that looks the most fun and exciting to you first. Physical attraction works a bit like that for grown-ups when they look for a partner; it's the first thing that makes them want to get to know someone better, kind of like a friendly spark that starts the conversation. While being kind and sharing laughs are what really keeps people together for a long time, that initial spark helps two people feel excited to start their adventure together.

title: Why can some animals be domesticated while others can't?
text: Think of animals like toys—some are easy to play with and share, while others are trickier and might break or not follow the rules. Animals that can be domesticated, like dogs or cows, usually like being around people, aren’t too picky about food, and don’t get scared easily. They’re also happy to live in groups and listen to a leader, which makes them good friends for humans. Animals that can’t be domesticated, like zebras or tigers, are often more nervous, need very special food or space, or prefer to be alone, so they don’t enjoy living with people or following our rules.

title: When you floor the gas in a car, why does your head get thrown back against the seat?
text: When you push the gas pedal all the way down, the car's engine makes the wheels spin really fast to push the car forward quickly, but your body wants to stay right where it is—like when you're sitting on a sled and someone gives you a sudden push from behind, your head leans back because the rest of you starts moving forward first.

title: Can you create a flashlight bright enough to shine completely through a person?
text: No, you cannot make a flashlight that shines completely through a person because our bodies are not see-through like glass—our skin, muscles, and bones are very good at blocking and absorbing light, so even the brightest flashlight beam would only make your skin glow a little bit red and would not pass out the other side.

title: How come as children most of us didn't enjoy certain flavors, but as adults we start craving and liking said flavors? (Veggies, dark chocolate, etc.)
text: Think of your taste buds like a team of tiny guards in your mouth, and when you're little, they're extra sensitive and shout really loudly about new or strong flavors—like the bitterness in veggies or dark chocolate—because they're trying to protect you from eating something that might be bad. As you grow up, those guards get used to more foods and stop shouting so much, so your brain learns that these flavors are actually safe and can be really tasty, especially when you notice they make you feel good and healthy.

title: when showering /swimming, why is it that only our hands and feet prune, and not the rest of our skin?
text: Think of your skin like a raincoat—most of it is really good at keeping water out, but your hands and feet have extra-thick skin that soaks up water like a sponge, making them wrinkle up to help you grip things better when they're wet.

title: What is happening when we suddenly forget something, then go back to a previous activity and remember it?
text: Imagine your brain is like a busy toy room where you're only holding one toy at a time—when you switch to a new toy, you put the old one down. Sometimes, when you walk into a different room to get the new toy, you forget the old one you wanted. Going back to the first room is like giving your brain the same clues it had before, helping it find the right toy again.

title: why do we have nightmares?
text: Nightmares are like scary movies that play in your head while you sleep, and they happen because your brain is trying to sort through all the things you felt or thought about during the day—like being worried about a test or seeing something frightening—and sometimes it mixes those feelings up into a scary story to help you practice dealing with them.

title: Why do most foods taste better when drunk or high?
text: When you're drunk or high, your brain gets a little mixed up and makes your senses, like taste and smell, feel stronger and more enjoyable, so foods can seem extra yummy even if they're just normal snacks.

title: How Do Iq tests work exactly?
text: IQ tests work by asking you a variety of puzzles and questions that check how well you can solve problems, remember things, understand words, and see patterns, and then they compare your score to lots of other people your age to give you a number that shows how you did compared to them.

title: How does math actually work in life and the universe?
text: Math is like a secret code that helps us understand patterns and solve puzzles in everything around us, from counting your toys to figuring out how planets move in space—it’s the special language the universe uses to make sense of itself.

title: Why does your stomach suddenly hurt from eating after a long period of not eating?
text: Imagine your stomach is like a little balloon that’s been empty and resting for a while—when you finally put food in it, it suddenly has to stretch and squeeze to get to work, which can feel a bit ouchy until it gets used to being busy again.

title: . Can energy turn in to matter?
text: Yes, energy can turn into matter! Think of energy like a superhero that can change into different forms—like how ice can melt into water. When a lot of energy is squeezed together in just the right way, it can create tiny particles of matter, almost like magic. Scientists do this in big machines called particle accelerators, where they smash energy together to make matter, showing that energy and matter are like two sides of the same coin.

title: What is Shareblue?
text: Shareblue is a news website that shares stories and opinions about politics, and it was created to support and promote the ideas of the Democratic Party in the United States.

title: Why do shows like The Daily Show and Full frontal take a commercial break just before the end of the programme, only to end the show seconds later?
text: They do that because the very last thing you see is often a short, funny clip or the host's final joke, and the show wants to make sure you stick around for it instead of changing the channel right when the commercials start—it's like putting a yummy dessert right after you finish your vegetables so you don't leave the table early.

title: How come sometimes a coin won't work on a vending machine, then after retrying it one or multiple times it will work eventually?
text: Think of a vending machine's coin slot like a tiny, very picky gatekeeper. It checks each coin for the right size, weight, and metal. Sometimes, even a good coin goes in a little crooked or bounces funny, so the gatekeeper gets confused and says "no." When you try again, you might drop it more smoothly, letting the gatekeeper check it properly and say "yes, you can pass."

title: How do sites that don't display ads make money?
text: Imagine a website is like a lemonade stand, but instead of selling lemonade, it gives away free lemonade to everyone who visits. To still make money, the stand might have a tip jar for donations, or it might sell special fancy cups next to the free lemonade. Websites that don't show ads work the same way—they give you something for free, but they make money in other sneaky spots, like by selling special extra features, getting donations, or collecting and selling helpful information about what people like, without ever saying your name.

title: With the recent information on Session's on Russia, why do we have to wait for him to resign? Can't we just go after him for treason or whatever and give him the harshest punishment for lying under oath?
text: We can't just go after someone for treason because that's a very specific and serious crime that involves helping an enemy during a war, which doesn't fit here. As for lying under oath, that's called perjury, and it's very hard to prove because you have to show the person knew they were lying and meant to do it. In big government investigations, things move slowly because there are lots of rules to follow to make sure everything is fair. So even if people are upset, the law has to take its time to gather all the evidence and build a strong case.

title: Why do some people stop liking something when it becomes popular/mainstream?
text: Imagine you have a favorite toy that you think is super special and just yours, but then suddenly everyone at school starts playing with the same toy—it might feel less special because it’s not just your secret favorite anymore, and sometimes when things get really popular, they change a little to please everyone, which can make them feel less unique to you.

title: why does the Big Bang mark the beginning of time and space? How can nothing exist before that?
text: Imagine the universe is like a movie playing on a TV screen—the Big Bang is the very first frame of that movie, and before that first frame, there's just nothing on the screen, not even a blank screen. Scientists say time and space started with the Big Bang because everything we know—all of space, all of time, and even the rules of how things work—began expanding from a tiny, super-hot point. Asking what was before the Big Bang is like asking what's north of the North Pole—there isn't a "before" because time itself didn't exist yet, so "before" doesn't have any meaning. It's a tricky idea because our brains are used to thinking that everything has a beginning and something before it, but for the universe, the Big Bang is where the story starts.

title: What is happening when a game is loading?
text: When a game is loading, it's like your computer or console is unpacking all the toys and setting up the playground before you can start playing—it's gathering all the pictures, sounds, and rules from the game's storage and putting them in the right spots in its memory so everything is ready to run smoothly when you press start.

title: How comes so many recipes call for a baking temperature of 350-400F?
text: Many recipes use temperatures between 350°F and 400°F because it’s a sweet spot that cooks food thoroughly without burning it—it’s like a “Goldilocks” zone for baking where the heat is just right to turn ingredients golden brown and delicious.

title: Why do production outfits ask bystanders to sign release forms for their faces to be shown, but vloggers don't have to?
text: Think of it like a game of tag: a big movie crew is like playing in an organized game with lots of rules—they have to get everyone’s permission to be "it" so no one gets upset later. A vlogger is more like a kid playing tag in a public park; if you’re out in a public place where anyone can see you, they usually don’t need to ask because you’re already part of the background of everyday life, just like trees or sidewalks.

title: How exactly was Russia allegedly involved with the Presidential election and what did they do?
text: Imagine you and a friend are having a contest to see who can build the best block tower, but another kid from across the playground wants your friend to win. That kid doesn't come over and build the tower for your friend, but instead, he might sneak over and quietly knock some of your blocks over, or he might tell other kids made-up stories about your tower being wobbly so they won't help you. In a very similar way, the U.S. government found that Russia didn't change vote counts, but they did two main things to try to cause trouble and help one candidate: they stole and leaked embarrassing emails to make people upset, and they used fake social media accounts to spread lots of angry arguments and untrue news stories to make Americans fight with each other and distrust the election.

title: Why do so many people recommend "no-kill" shelters for adopting a pet? Isn't it better to adopt from a "kill" shelter - you're actually saving a life?
text: That's a great question! Think of it like this: both kinds of shelters are trying to help animals, but they work in different ways. A "no-kill" shelter is like a very crowded, full hotel—they can only take in new animals when other animals get adopted, so sometimes they have to turn animals away. A "kill" shelter (often called an "open-admission" shelter) is like a big emergency room—they never turn away any animal, even if they are sick or there's no space, but that sometimes means they have to make the very sad choice to put animals to sleep when they run out of room. When you adopt from *any* shelter, you are saving a life! Adopting from an open-admission shelter directly frees up a space for another animal to come in and get a chance, while adopting from a no-kill shelter helps them make room so they can rescue more animals from those crowded emergency rooms. So really, the best place to adopt is whichever one has the pet that's right for you, because every adoption helps.

title: Do we know if all human brains perceive color the same way?
text: We can't be sure if everyone sees colors exactly the same way because we can't look through each other's eyes, but we do know that most people's eyes work the same way with special cells that pick up red, green, and blue light, so we all agree that grass is green and the sky is blue—even if your green might look a little different in your head than mine.

title: What is the limit of our brain?
text: Think of your brain like a super-smart computer that never gets full, but sometimes it gets a little slow or forgets things because it's busy. It can learn new stuff every day, but it can't pay attention to everything at once—just like you can't listen to two songs at the same time without getting mixed up. So, the limit isn't really about running out of space, but more about how much it can focus on or remember at one time.

title: Should I really be avoiding processed foods? What does it mean for foods to be "processed"?
text: Think of processed foods like toys that come already built from a box—they're changed from how they're found in nature to make them last longer, taste different, or be easier to eat. Some changes are small and okay, like freezing peas or turning milk into yogurt, but other changes add lots of extra sugar, salt, and fake stuff that aren't very good for your body. You don't have to avoid them completely, but it's healthier to eat more foods that look like they just came from a farm or a tree, like fruits, veggies, and nuts, because they give your body the best fuel to grow and play.

title: Why are some people more likely to have sleep paralysis, while others never have it or have only experienced it once?
text: Imagine your brain and body are like a team that needs to switch jobs at bedtime: your brain (the thinker) should stay awake to dream, but your body (the mover) should take a nap so you don’t act out your dreams. Sometimes, if you’re very tired, stressed, or your sleep schedule is mixed up, your brain wakes up too early while your body is still napping. That’s sleep paralysis—you’re awake but can’t move. Some people have this happen more often because they might have sleep problems, lots of worry, or a family that experiences it too, while others have better sleep habits or just get lucky and their brain and body wake up at the same time.

title: Why aren't consumer computers "instant" yet, in terms of the basic functions like booting up, opening up programs, etc? I mean literally instant, with zero delay following a mouse click. Will they ever be?
text: Think of your computer like a big, busy toy box. When you turn it on, it has to take out every single toy and put it in just the right spot before you can play—that's the boot-up time. Opening a program is like digging for a specific toy in that box; even if you know where it is, you still have to grab it. Computers aren't instant because they have to read instructions from their storage, which is much slower than their brain (the processor), and they have to do many little steps in order. They might get much, much faster—like having a super-organized toy box right at your fingertips—but to be truly instant with zero delay for everything would be like having a toy magically appear in your hand the moment you think of it, which is probably impossible because electricity and light themselves take tiny amounts of time to move around.

title: Why in politics do parties have to speak to the speaker and not to the opposing party?
text: In a debate, it’s like being in a classroom where everyone has to raise their hand and talk to the teacher instead of shouting across the room—the speaker is like that teacher, making sure everyone takes turns, follows the rules, and stays respectful so that important discussions don’t turn into noisy arguments.

title: If chess is considered a sport, why not checkers?
text: Chess is considered a sport because it's played in serious competitions with official rules, requires a lot of brain training and strategy, and even has an international organization like the Olympics for games, but checkers is often seen as a simpler game that many people play just for fun without as many big tournaments or as much complex thinking.

title: Why is the blue ink very common for writing, but when it comes to printing, black ink is extremely common?
text: Blue ink is popular for writing because it stands out clearly against white paper and looks friendly, while black ink is used most in printing because it’s darker, crisper, and works better for small text and important documents without looking faded.

title: How can we distinguish something that is real news and fake news?
text: Think of news like a story someone tells you—real news is like when your teacher tells you what happened at school, because she was there and can show you pictures or ask other teachers who saw it too. Fake news is like when a friend makes up a silly rumor on the playground but can’t prove it. To tell them apart, check who is telling the story: real news comes from trusted people or places that check facts, just like you’d trust a grown-up over a stranger. Also, look for proof, like photos or other people saying the same thing, and if a story makes you feel super angry or scared right away, it might be fake trying to trick you.

title: Why does vision blur when the skin next to an eye is stretched?
text: When you gently pull the skin near your eye, you're also tugging a little on your eyeball itself, which changes its shape just enough that the light coming in doesn't focus perfectly on the back of your eye, making things look blurry for a moment.

title: If a mirror reflects all light and the color white reflects all wavelengths of light then why is there a difference between a mirror and a white sheet of paper?
text: A mirror is like a super smooth pond that reflects light like a bouncing ball, sending it back in the same neat order so you see a clear picture, while white paper is like bumpy gravel that scatters light in all directions like a messy splash, so you only see its bright white color without a reflection.

title: How can antivirus companies can analyse new and powerful viruses without getting themselves infected ?
text: Antivirus companies use special safe rooms called "sandboxes" that are like super-secure digital playpens—they let the virus run around inside to see what it does, but the walls are so strong it can't escape to hurt the real computer.

title: What is the point of ads that infect your device with viruses?
text: The point of those bad ads is to sneak onto your device like a tiny, invisible thief so they can steal things from you, like your passwords, your pictures, or even your money, or sometimes they just want to break your things and make your device act very strange and slow.

title: Why is the weather usually pleasant after a thunderstorm?
text: After a thunderstorm, the weather often feels nice because the storm acts like a big cleaning machine for the air—it washes away dust and pollen with rain, and the lightning helps freshen the air too. The dark clouds move out, letting the sun warm things up again, and the leftover rain cools everything down, making it feel comfortably fresh and clean.

title: what happens when we get headaches and why does a glass of water sometimes cure it?
text: A headache is like your brain's way of saying "ouch!" even though your brain itself can't feel pain—it's actually the muscles and blood vessels around your head and neck getting upset, often because you're tired, stressed, or your body needs something. Sometimes, especially if you haven't had enough to drink, those parts get a little dry and cranky, so drinking a glass of water helps them relax and feel better, which makes the headache go away.

title: How is the answer to this question not 84?
text:
If you have 12 apples and you give 7 to a friend, you have 5 apples left.  
Sometimes questions try to trick you by asking something like "What is 12 times 7?" but if the real question was about subtraction, the answer wouldn't be 84.  
So the answer isn't 84 because the question might be about something else, like taking away apples instead of multiplying them.

title: Do people without Nielsen boxes affect viewership ratings? Does recording a show and watching it later increase viewership counts?
text: Yes, people without Nielsen boxes still affect viewership in a big way, but not directly in the ratings you usually hear about—it's like if your teacher only asked a few kids in class what their favorite book was, but the whole class's opinions still matter to the librarian buying books for the school. Networks and advertisers care about everyone, but the official ratings mostly come from those Nielsen boxes. As for recording and watching later, yes, that often does count! Many Nielsen boxes now track that, and if you watch the show within a certain time (like up to a week later), it's usually added to the ratings, helping the show look popular.

title: Will a more obese person burn more calories with the same daily activity as a thinner person strictly because of the amount of effort necessary to keep up?
text: Yes, because moving a bigger body takes more work, just like pushing a heavy wagon is harder than pushing a light one—your muscles have to use more energy to carry the extra weight around, so they burn more calories doing the same activities.

title: Why is parental approval so important when we're choosing a partner? Are there other species that exhibit this behavior?
text: Think of your parents like your very first teachers who know you really well—they want to make sure you pick a partner who will be kind and help you be happy, just like they’ve tried to do. Other animals do this too, like some birds where the parents will chase away a suitor they don’t like, because they’re looking out for their family’s safety and happiness.

title: How can NASCAR say they use "stock cars" when the cars used are far from being "stock"?
text: NASCAR cars used to be just like the ones you could buy at a dealership, but over time teams changed them to be faster and safer, so now they're really only "stock" because they look like the regular cars on the outside.

title: How can the economy keep growing every year if the planet has a finite amount of resources?
text: Think of the economy like a big sandbox where we build things. The sandbox has a limited amount of sand (that's our planet's finite resources), but we can get better at building by using the same sand in smarter ways—like building taller, more interesting castles with the same handful of sand, or even finding new types of sand we didn't notice before. Growth doesn't always mean using more stuff; it can mean making cooler, more useful things with what we already have, or learning to share and reuse our toys better.

title: Do loud noises travel slightly faster than very quiet noises or does loud noise just travel further at the same speed?
text:
Sound always travels at the same speed through the air, like a car on a road with a strict speed limit, so loud noises and quiet noises travel side-by-side at the same speed.  
The difference is that loud noises are like a big, strong shout that you can hear from far away, while quiet noises are like a tiny whisper that disappears quickly, so loud noises travel further even though they don't go any faster.

title: How does the Fourth Amendment prevent government reach into government cell phones?
text: The Fourth Amendment is like a rule that says the police can't look through your stuff without a good reason, and this includes your cell phone. Even though the phone is owned by the government if you work for them, the rule still protects your personal messages, photos, and information on it. This means a boss or police officer usually needs to get special permission from a judge to search it, unless there's a really urgent emergency. So, it keeps your private things on the phone safe from unnecessary government snooping.

title: Why is it that we develop a tolerance to drugs, but not sex/masturbation?
text: Think of your brain like a party where certain activities invite special guests called "receptors." When you take a drug, it brings a huge, overwhelming crowd of guests that your brain isn't used to, so it starts removing some party invitations (receptors) to keep things calm—that's tolerance, meaning you need more of the drug next time to get the same big crowd. With sex or masturbation, your brain releases its own natural party guests in a balanced way that it's designed to handle, so it doesn't need to remove invitations, and you don't build up the same kind of tolerance.

title: From what I gather, Wikipedia seems to be a fairly neutral source. What prevents the polarization of facts on Wikipedia?
text: Imagine Wikipedia is a giant coloring book that everyone in the world can draw in, but there are lots of grown-up helpers watching. If someone tries to color a dog bright purple and say "all dogs are purple," the helpers quickly check their real pictures of dogs and change it back to brown or black or white. They also make a rule that you can only use colors from the "real fact" crayon box, not from the "just my opinion" crayon box. Because so many people are watching and fixing pages all the time, it’s really hard for one person to make everything look the way only they want it to—the helpers and other colorers keep things looking mostly right for everyone.

title: How does hashing work for single value like the letter "a"?
text: Think of hashing like a special blender for information: if you put the letter "a" into it, the blender chops and mixes it into a fixed-length jumble of letters and numbers that looks nothing like the original "a", and every time you put "a" in, you always get the exact same jumble out.

title: How did people slack off/waste time at their desks before the Internet or cellphones were invented?
text: Before computers and phones, people found sneaky ways to take little breaks at their desks, like pretending to be very busy organizing papers, doodling on notepads, reading the newspaper or a book hidden in a drawer, staring out the window while looking thoughtful, taking extra long trips to the water cooler, or having extra-long chats with coworkers about anything but work.

title: Why social media apps take up so much storage?
text: Social media apps take up a lot of storage because they are constantly collecting and saving things on your phone, like every picture and video you see, all the conversations you have, and even information about what you click on, so they can show it to you again quickly without having to download it every single time.

title: Why are some Moles cancerous while others can be completely harmless?
text: Think of your skin like a big garden, and moles are just little clumps of extra plants that sometimes grow. Most of the time, these clumps are friendly and stay small and quiet—they’re harmless. But sometimes, a few of the plants in that clump start growing in a wild, messy way and don’t listen to the garden’s rules to stop. When that happens, the mole can turn into a problem called cancer, because those wild cells can spread and cause trouble. Doctors check moles for signs of this wild growth, like if they change shape, color, or size, to catch the naughty ones early.

title: What does the 4th dimension look like, and how would we perceive it?
text: Imagine you're a flat drawing on a piece of paper—you can only see left, right, forward, and back, but you can't see up or down at all. If a 3D object like a ball passed through your flat paper world, you wouldn't see the whole ball—you'd just see a dot that grows into a circle and then shrinks back to a dot. For us in our 3D world, the 4th dimension is like that "up" direction we can't point to. We can't see it directly, but if a 4D object passed through our space, we'd see it as a 3D shape that mysteriously changes, like a cube that appears out of nowhere, grows, twists, and vanishes. We'd only catch 3D "slices" of it, just like the flat drawing only sees 2D slices of the ball.

title: Assuming a consistently dark environment, how do our bodies know when it is time to wake up/that we have had enough rest?
text: Even in total darkness, your body has a tiny built-in clock in your brain called the circadian rhythm, which runs on a roughly 24-hour schedule. This clock uses cues from your past days—like when you normally see sunlight, eat, or move around—to guess what time it is. It also listens to your body’s tiredness from the day’s activities, so when you’ve had enough sleep, your brain slowly turns down the sleep chemicals and turns up the awake ones, telling your body it’s time to wake up.

title: If humans were to colonize a new planet and could only send "X" number of people. What is the minimum number of people we would need to send in order to create a genetically diverse population?
text: To make a new population on another planet without everyone being too closely related, scientists think you'd need at least about 80 to 100 people, but to be really safe and avoid problems, a group of around 500 is a much better idea. This is because you need enough different genes so that future generations stay healthy—if you start with too few people, their kids and grandkids might all inherit the same rare diseases or weaknesses. Think of it like having a big box of crayons: if you only have a few colors, you can't draw as many different pictures, but with lots of colors, you can create anything you want!

title: How do banks know if a check has already been deposited?
text: Banks keep track of checks by using special numbers on the check, like a check number and your account number, and when you deposit a check, they mark it in their computer system so they know it's been used and can't be deposited again.

title: Why do they still make complicated stop-motion movies if there is more-efficient animation software available?
text: Stop-motion is like making a movie out of a big, moving craft project, and even though drawing on a computer is faster, some people love the special, real-world magic of seeing actual puppets and clay come to life, because it feels warm and unique, like a favorite handmade toy.

title: The moon is bright enough to be seen from 240,000 miles away even in daytime, how could astronauts look directly at it during the lunar space landing?
text: The Moon is bright when we see it from Earth because it's reflecting the Sun's light through the dark sky, but up close on the Moon's surface, the ground is actually a dark gray color like dusty asphalt, so it doesn't glare like snow or a white sand beach. Also, the astronauts landed on the daytime side of the Moon, but the sky is always black there because the Moon has no air to scatter sunlight, so even though the Sun itself is extremely bright and they couldn't look at it, the Moon's surface just looked like dim, rocky ground in the shadow of their spacesuits, which had special gold-coated visors to protect their eyes.

title: What is (if there is one) the difference between machine learning and AI?
text: Think of AI as a big, smart robot that can do lots of things, like play chess or talk to you, and machine learning is like the special brain-training homework that helps the robot learn how to do those things all by itself.

title: How can they tell what started a wild fire?
text: They can figure out what started a wildfire by looking for clues at the very beginning, like a detective. Firefighters and investigators go to the spot where the fire first began and search for things that don't belong, such as a campfire ring, a cigarette butt, or a broken power line. They also check the weather to see if lightning struck there, because lightning is a natural fire starter. By putting all these clues together, they can usually tell if it was caused by people or by nature.

title: What causes the American South and Midwest to have so many tornadoes, and why are they so relatively rare everywhere else in the world?
text: Think of the United States like a big mixing bowl for air, where the American South and Midwest are right in the middle of the bowl. Warm, wet air from the Gulf of Mexico floats north and meets cold, dry air coming down from Canada, and then another layer of fast-moving air high up in the sky comes over the Rocky Mountains and acts like a big spoon that stirs everything together. When these three different kinds of air crash into each other, they can create powerful spinning thunderstorms called supercells, which are the kind that often make tornadoes. Most other places in the world don’t have all three of these ingredients—the warm wet air, the cold dry air, and the fast high-up air—meeting in just the right way at the same time and in such a big flat area, which is why big tornadoes are much rarer everywhere else.

title: Why are we always told to make sure someone doesn't swallow their tongue when they go unconscious or have a seizure, when it isn't actually possible to swallow our tongues?
text: That's a great question! It's true that you can't actually swallow your tongue because it's firmly attached to the bottom of your mouth. The warning comes from a mix-up of words and a real danger. When someone is unconscious or having a seizure, their muscles can become very relaxed, including the tongue. The tongue can flop back and block the airway—the tube we breathe through—like a big, soft plug. So, people really mean "don't let their tongue block their throat," but over time it got shortened to "swallow their tongue." The most important thing to do is to gently roll the person on their side, which lets the tongue fall forward and keeps their airway clear so they can breathe safely.

title: What determines the noise or visual pattern of TV static?
text: TV static, also called "snow," happens because your TV is trying to listen for a signal from a TV station, but it can't find one clearly. Instead, it picks up tiny bits of energy and electricity that are always floating in the air and inside the TV itself, like invisible whispers. These random bits get turned into the random black-and-white dots and the fuzzy hissing sound you see and hear.

title: Why is "talked with Russia so bad? Isn't WHAT they talked about more important?/A Swede.
text: Talking with Russia isn't always bad, but for many countries, especially neighbors like Sweden, it's tricky because Russia has a history of not keeping its promises and using talks to get what it wants without giving much back. Think of it like talking to a school bully who often lies—what you talk about is important, but you have to be very careful because you can't always trust that they mean what they say. For Sweden, which wants to keep itself and its friends safe, talking might only be a good idea if it's very clear that Russia is being honest and not just trying to trick them.

title: What causes pain during a headache?
text: Imagine your brain doesn't actually feel pain itself, but the things around it—like the lining of your head, your blood vessels, and the muscles in your neck and scalp—can get upset. A headache happens when these parts get squeezed, stretched, or irritated, which sends "ouch" messages to your brain, making you feel the pain in your head.

title: Why do puppies always want to lick your face?
text: Puppies lick your face because it's their way of showing they love you and think you're part of their family, kind of like how they would lick their mom's face to say they're hungry or to say hello when they were very tiny.

title: What happens to insects in winter?
text: In winter, many insects hide in cozy spots like under leaves, inside tree bark, or underground to sleep through the cold, kind of like a long nap called hibernation; some, like monarch butterflies, fly to warmer places, while others lay eggs that can survive the winter and hatch when it gets warm again.

title: How did Scientists create a 1.4 mb strand of DNA?
text: Scientists created a 1.4 megabyte strand of DNA by treating it like a super tiny computer hard drive—they turned the 1s and 0s of digital files (like text and images) into the four-letter alphabet of DNA (A, T, C, G), then used special machines to build the DNA strand piece by piece, just like stringing together microscopic beads in the right order.

title: Does drinking a lot of water dilute stomach acid?
text: Drinking a lot of water can temporarily make your stomach acid a little weaker, just like adding water to lemon juice makes it less sour, but your stomach is really smart and quickly gets back to work making more acid so it can keep digesting your food properly.

title: What causes a human to want to pick at their scabs?
text: When you get a cut, your body makes a hard, crusty scab to protect it while new skin grows underneath—but sometimes that scab can feel itchy or just interesting to touch, so you might pick at it without really thinking, almost like how it’s hard to ignore a loose tooth.

title: Why do candles smell strongest when you blow them out?
text: When you blow out a candle, the hot wax keeps evaporating for a moment, sending a big puff of smelly wax vapor into the air that you can easily smell, while when it's burning, some of the smell gets used up by the flame.

title: Why do bacteria/viruses/parasites that are host dependent eventually kill their host?
text:
Imagine you're having a playdate and you really love the snacks at your friend's house—you might eat so much that there's nothing left for your friend, and then the playdate has to end.  
Bacteria, viruses, and parasites are like tiny visitors that need your body to live and make more of themselves, but they don't always know when to stop.  
If they grow too much or spread too fast, they can damage important parts of your body, like making it hard to breathe or stealing all your energy, and that can make you very sick or even cause death.  
They aren't trying to kill you on purpose—it's just that their survival sometimes accidentally breaks the things your body needs to stay alive.

title: Why does the History Channel not show more historical programming?
text: The History Channel used to show lots of shows about things like wars and ancient buildings, but they found out that more people watch shows about things like treasure hunters, aliens, and big trucks, so they changed to get more viewers and make more money from ads.

title: Why are headaches and toothaches much less tolerable other kinds of body pain?
text: Think of your body like a busy city with lots of streets (nerves) carrying messages to the main headquarters (your brain). Headaches and toothaches happen right near the headquarters, so the pain signals don't have to travel far and arrive very loud and clear, making them hard to ignore. Other pains, like a scraped knee, happen on a street far away, so the message is a little quieter by the time it reaches headquarters.

title: How do musicians come up with chord progressions?
text: Musicians come up with chord progressions a bit like building with colorful blocks that each have a special feeling—some sound happy, some sad, some like they want to go somewhere else. They often start by picking a key, which is like choosing a family of notes that all sound good together. Then they experiment by playing different chords from that family in an order that tells a musical story, using their ears to find what sounds nice, exciting, or emotional. Sometimes they copy patterns from songs they love, and other times they just mess around until something cool happens!

title: If Potassium Iodide (KI) protects us from radiation, why we are not given KI before CT scans ?
text: Potassium iodide only protects one specific part of your body, the thyroid gland in your neck, from one specific type of radiation, which comes from a radioactive form of iodine. CT scans use a completely different kind of radiation, like powerful X-rays, that go through your whole body to take pictures; potassium iodide doesn't block that kind at all, so taking it for a CT scan would be like wearing a raincoat to protect you from the sun—it's just the wrong tool for the job.

title: How deep into the Earth could humans dig? (If any equipment was available)
text: If we could use any digging machine we wanted, we could only dig down about 40 miles into the Earth—which is like trying to poke through just the very thin, crispy skin of an apple. Even though the Earth is nearly 8,000 miles across, the deeper you go, the hotter and squishier everything gets. Long before we reached the center, the rock would get so hot and under so much pressure that it would act like a thick, gooey paste, and any hole we tried to make would just squeeze shut behind our drill.

title: Why can't we just surgically remove all the fat in a morbidly obese person in addition to the gastric bypass surgery?
text: Think of your body like a big, busy city where fat is like the storage warehouses for energy—if we took out all the warehouses at once, the delivery trucks (your blood and hormones) would have nowhere to go and could cause traffic jams and problems everywhere, plus your skin would be like a giant empty sack with nothing to support it, which could make you very sick instead of helping you get healthy.

title: What category of taste does mint fall into because it doesn't seem to fit with any of the five tastes? (sweet, sour, bitter, salty and umami)
text: Mint isn't one of the five main tastes—it's actually a feeling! The coolness from mint comes from a special trick: a chemical in it gently tells the nerves in your mouth that they're cold, even when they're not. So, while your taste buds are busy detecting things like sweet or bitter, your touch and temperature nerves are saying, "Wow, that's chilly!" That's why mint feels refreshing but doesn't have its own taste category.

title: If an elderly person is, literally, as fit and healthy as possible, what will eventually kill them?
text: Even if someone takes perfect care of themselves their whole life, their body is like a machine that slowly wears out from being used—tiny parts inside their cells stop copying perfectly, and over many, many years, this adds up until something simple, like their heart just getting too tired to beat or their brain forgetting how to tell their lungs to breathe, is what finally stops the machine.

title: Why does eating spicy food burn?
text: Eating spicy food burns because of a trick played on your brain by a chemical called capsaicin, which is found in peppers. This chemical doesn't actually burn you like fire, but it sticks to special sensors in your mouth that normally warn you about heat. When these sensors are triggered, they send a "hot" signal to your brain, making your mouth feel like it's on fire even though it's not. Your body reacts by sweating and sometimes making your nose run, trying to cool itself down from a heat that isn't really there.

title: How are credit card numbers validated?
text: Credit card numbers are checked using a special math trick called the Luhn algorithm, which is like a secret code that helps computers quickly spot mistakes. Imagine you have a string of numbers, and you double every other digit starting from the end; if doubling gives you a two-digit number, you add those digits together. Then you add up all the numbers, and if the total ends in a zero, the card number passes the test! This doesn't mean the card is real or has money, but it catches common typos right away, like if you accidentally press the wrong button when typing the number.

title: why/how does your nose continuously produce so much snot when you or sick or have allergies?
text: When you're sick or have allergies, your body thinks there are tiny invaders like germs or pollen inside your nose, so it sends extra blood and defenders called mucus to help trap and wash them away, which makes your nose feel snotty and runny.

title: Why are ejaculations so much more powerful when a guy has been horny or really turned on?
text: When a guy gets really turned on, his body gets extra excited and builds up more of the special liquid that comes out during an ejaculation, kind of like filling a water balloon more and more—so when it finally happens, it comes out with more force and feels stronger.

title: - Ryzen Cpu's? What's all the fuss about?
text: Imagine your computer's brain, called a CPU, is like a team of workers building a toy castle. For a long time, one company, Intel, mostly had teams with a few really strong, fast workers. Then AMD, the other company, made Ryzen teams with lots and lots of workers. Even if each Ryzen worker is a tiny bit slower, having so many means they can build way more parts of the castle at the same time, often making the whole job faster for less money. That’s why people get excited—Ryzen often gives you more power for your pocket money, whether you’re playing games, doing homework, or watching videos.

title: If radiation exposure causes cancer, why do they use it to treat cancer patients? Won't it just guarantee they will develop more cancer in the future?
text: That's a great question! Think of radiation like a powerful water gun that can be used in two different ways: if you spray it all over the place, it can make a big mess, but if you aim it very carefully at a single dirty spot, you can clean it up. When doctors treat cancer with radiation, they aim it super precisely at the cancer cells to break them apart and stop them from growing, and they use a shield to protect the healthy parts of your body. Yes, there is a tiny chance it could cause a new problem later, but the big cancer you have right now is a much bigger danger, so doctors use the radiation to fight that first.

title: Why does the last 15% of my phone battery life disappear so much faster?
text: Think of your phone battery like a bucket of water with a tiny hole in the bottom—the battery percentage is how much water is left. When the bucket is full, the hole is at the bottom, so the water drains out slowly and steadily. But as the water gets lower, the hole is actually moving up the side of the bucket, making the last bit of water drain out much faster because there's less pressure pushing it out. In your phone, the battery's chemicals get tired and can't hold energy as well when they're almost empty, so that last 15% seems to disappear in a hurry.

title: Why are most DVD and video game cases still so big?
text: Think of a DVD or game case like a cereal box—it needs to be big enough to catch your eye on the store shelf and show off cool artwork, even though the actual disc inside is pretty small. The bigger case also makes it harder to steal and gives you a nice place to read the story or instructions on the back.

title: Travelling from Canada to Asia. Why can't planes fly west instead? Wouldn't it be faster?
text: Planes do fly west when going to Asia from Canada, but they often take a longer curved path that looks north on a map because it’s actually shorter—the Earth is round, so flying over the Arctic is a more direct route than following a straight line on a flat map.

title: Why do zebras have a black and white hide? It seems as if these colors wouldn't be a suitable camouflage for their surrounding environment
text: Zebras have black and white stripes not to blend into the background like some animals do, but to confuse their main predators, lions and hyenas, especially when they're in a big group. When a bunch of zebras run together, all those swirling stripes make it hard for a hunter to pick out just one zebra to chase. It's also tricky for biting flies, like horseflies, because the stripes mess up their vision and make it harder for them to land on the zebra for a bite.

title: How do they declare certain aquatic organisms as extinct, when we haven't explored a huge majority of the oceans?
text: Scientists look for the creatures in all the places they used to live, and if nobody has seen one for a very, very long time—even with special tools like submarines and cameras—they sadly decide it’s probably gone forever, just like when you lose a toy and can’t find it anywhere even after searching all the spots it could be.

title: Why do we get black circles under our eyes when we don't get enough sleep?
text: Think of the skin under your eyes like a very thin, stretchy balloon. When you don't get enough sleep, your body gets tired and the blood in the tiny tubes under your eyes moves slower and can bunch up there, making the skin look darker and purpleish-blue, like seeing a juice stain through a napkin. Also, when you're tired, your whole face can get a little puffy, which can make shadows under your eyes look even darker.

title: How is it determined whether or not citizens of a country need a visa to travel to another country?
text: It’s like deciding who gets to come into your clubhouse. Countries make agreements with each other about who can visit easily. If two countries are good friends and trust each other, they often say, “You don’t need a special permission slip (visa) to visit.” But if a country worries someone might stay without asking or cause trouble, they might require a visa to check people first. They look at things like safety, whether visitors usually follow the rules, and if lots of people travel back and forth.

title: How do Atomic bombs work? Is it just one atom torn apart?
