text: In movies, illegal fights are like secret games where people watch fighters compete in hidden places, and betting happens quietly with hand signals or whispers to avoid getting caught by the police.

title: Why do we get that tingling feeling when we hit our "funny bone"?
text: That tingling feeling happens because you're actually squishing a nerve, not a bone! Your funny bone is a spot on your elbow where a nerve called the ulnar nerve is very close to the skin, with just a little bit of bone to protect it. When you bump it hard, you press the nerve against that bone. Nerves are like telephone wires that send messages to your brain, and when you squish one, it gets confused and sends a bunch of mixed-up signals. Your brain gets messages that feel like buzzing, tingling, or even a little pain, mostly in your pinky and ring finger, because that's the part of your hand that nerve talks to.

title: Why do powerful countries continue to make nuclear weapons even though very few can cause nuclear winter?
text: Even though just a few big bombs could cause a very cold, dark "nuclear winter," powerful countries keep making more because they think having the most weapons makes them safer—like in a game where no one wants to start a fight because everyone knows they would get hurt back just as badly.

title: Why do certain wild animals (whales, dolphins, etc.) that are otherwise predators try and help humans they encounter?
text: Imagine you're a really smart animal like a dolphin or a whale, and you see a human splashing in the water—you might think they're a strange, clumsy animal that's in trouble, so you help them because you're curious and kind, just like how you might help a puppy that got lost.

title: Why is there a gigantic desert in North-Afrika and Saudi-Arabia but not in India?
text: Imagine the Earth wearing a big, sandy belt around its middle—that's where most deserts are, and North Africa and Saudi Arabia sit right in the middle of that belt. This happens because the sun shines the strongest there, heating the air so much that it rises and leaves behind very little rain, making it super dry and sandy. India is also near that sunny belt, but it has a giant "rain helper" called the Himalayas—these huge mountains block wet winds from the ocean and squeeze out all the rain over India, keeping it green instead of turning into a desert.

title: Why can we smell coffee in our urine but not other liquids?
text: When you drink coffee, your body breaks it down and some of the strong-smelling parts end up in your pee, kind of like how a food's smell can stick on your hands after you eat it—other drinks don't have those same smelly parts, so your pee doesn't pick up their scent.

title: Why does coffee make me high strung and twitchy but tea doesn't?
text: Coffee has a lot more caffeine than tea, and it gets into your body much faster, which is like suddenly shouting "WAKE UP!" to your brain and making your body feel jumpy, while tea gives you a gentler, slower boost that's more like a friendly tap on the shoulder.

title: Why do over the counter pharmaceuticals (i.e. Tylenol) split the recommended dose between two capsules instead of one?
text: They split the dose into two capsules because your body can only use a little bit of the medicine at a time, and taking too much at once can hurt your liver or stomach; taking two smaller pills a few hours apart gives your body a steady, safe amount of medicine to help you feel better without getting overwhelmed.

title: How much heat does a pre-heated oven lose when you open it up to put in the food?
text: Think of your oven like a cozy, warm room and opening the door is like opening a window on a cold day—all the warm air whooshes out and cooler air rushes in to take its place. In just a few seconds of opening the oven, a huge amount of that heat escapes, and the oven’s temperature can drop by 100 degrees or more. The oven then has to work hard, like a little heater turning back on, to warm everything up again.

title: How are meteorologists able to forecast the weather 15+ days in advance? How often are those forecasts accurate?
text: Meteorologists use powerful computers that act like giant weather brains, taking in lots of information from weather stations, satellites, and balloons to predict what the atmosphere will do. For a forecast 15 days away, they run their computer programs many times with tiny changes to the starting information to see all the possible ways the weather might go, like looking at many different possible futures. However, that far ahead, small changes can lead to very different outcomes, so the forecast becomes less about exact details and more about general trends, like whether a whole region might be warmer or cooler than average. Those long-range forecasts are much less accurate than your daily weather report and should be taken as a very rough guess that will change as the days get closer.

title: Why is day trading of stocks a thing if its essentially a zero sum game?
text: Day trading is like playing a game of hot potato with stocks, where people try to buy low and sell high very quickly, and it keeps happening because everyone thinks they can be the one to outsmart the others and grab a profit before the music stops.

title: Why did older video games use checkpoints or locations to have to save your game instead of an options menu button like is most common now?
text: Older video games used checkpoints because the game cartridges and memory cards back then had very little space to store your progress, so the game could only save at certain spots, like after you beat a tricky level, which was simpler and used less space than letting you save anywhere you wanted.

title: What affects how rare & aggressive cancer is?
text: How rare or aggressive a cancer is depends mostly on where it starts in your body and how mixed up its instructions become, kind of like if a recipe book got messy. Some types of cancer are simply more common, like certain weeds in a garden. How fast and mean it grows depends on how broken the cells are—if they forget how to stop dividing and how to stay in their proper place, they can spread quickly and be harder to stop.

title: Why African Americans are not given the prefix of their country of origin while European's are?
text: That's a great question! The main reason is that for many African Americans, the specific countries their ancestors came from were lost due to the history of slavery, where records weren't kept and families were separated, so over time they formed a new cultural identity in America. For many people with European heritage, it's easier to trace family history back to a specific country like Italy or Ireland, so they might use those labels. It's not a rule, though—today, people whose families come from places like Nigeria or Jamaica often do use those prefixes if they know and feel connected to that heritage.

title: What does https everywhere do?
text: HTTPS Everywhere is like a special helper for your web browser that makes sure you always use the safest, most locked path when visiting websites, so that strangers can't peek at what you're doing or saying online.

title: What is dissolved carbon dioxide?
text: Dissolved carbon dioxide is like invisible bubbles of soda that mix into water, just like when you stir sugar into lemonade and it disappears but you can still taste it.

title: Why do connection speed sites like Ookla always have higher speeds than actual download speeds?
text: Think of it like a race track: Ookla measures how fast your car can go on an empty track, but when you actually download something, it's like driving in traffic with other cars, stoplights, and detours, so you can't go as fast.

title: Why do people consider MSG to be bad for health?
text: Some people think MSG is bad because a long time ago, a doctor wrote a letter saying it gave him headaches, and even though science says it's safe, that idea stuck around like a scary story that's hard to forget.

title: how does the new internet bill that Reddit hates so much work? Will I actually be able to call and request any person's web history? How will companies take advantage of this?
text: The new internet bill is like making a rule that your internet company has to keep a list of every website you visit, and then they can sell that list to other companies who want to show you ads for things they think you like. You won't be able to call and ask for a specific person's history—that list is sold in big, mixed-up bundles to advertisers, not shared with individuals. Companies will take advantage by using that information to send you very targeted ads, which can feel creepy because it might seem like they know exactly what you've been looking at online.

title: Why are body fluids salty?
text: Your body fluids are salty because they contain something called salt, which is made of tiny parts called sodium and chloride that help your cells work properly, just like how batteries need the right stuff inside to make toys run.

title: Why is there a double dribble rule?
text: Imagine you're playing basketball and you're holding the ball while running—that's not allowed, so you have to bounce it to move. The double dribble rule is there to make sure you don't get an unfair advantage by stopping your dribble and then starting to bounce it again, which would make it really hard for others to try and take the ball from you.

title: Why do new cars smell the way they do?
text: That new car smell comes from all the fresh materials inside, like the plastic on the dashboard, the glue holding things together, and the fabric on the seats—as these materials are new and haven't been used yet, they release a chemical smell that slowly fades away as the car gets older.

title: Where did the practice of putting Presidents on US money come from?
text: The idea started because putting a president's face on money is like giving the country a friendly and familiar picture to look at, kind of like how you might have a favorite teacher's drawing on the classroom wall. The very first U.S. coins showed a lady named Liberty, but after President Abraham Lincoln was sadly killed, people wanted to honor him, so they put his face on the penny. It made people feel good and remember him, so they started doing it for other important presidents, too, turning the money into a way to celebrate the country's history.

title: Why do we study Limits in Calculus?
text: We study limits in calculus because they help us understand how things change smoothly, like figuring out the exact speed of a car at one single moment even though we normally measure speed over a longer trip.

title: How is the position on the Earth's Surface determined by a GPS?
text: GPS works like a giant game of cosmic "Marco Polo" where your phone or GPS device shouts "Where am I?" and listens for replies from special satellites flying high above Earth. These satellites are constantly sending out signals that say exactly where they are and what time it is. Your GPS device catches these signals from at least four satellites, then uses the tiny differences in how long each signal took to arrive to figure out your exact spot—like measuring steps between friends on a playground to pinpoint where you're standing.

title: How does man "gets" enough vitamin D with lots of clothes on?
text: Even with clothes on, your skin can still make vitamin D from sunlight because some sunlight sneaks through the fabric, especially if it's thin or light-colored, and your face and hands are often uncovered.

title: Let's say I bought this big bulk of data from my local ISP under S.J.Res.34. What exactly am I looking at?
text: Imagine you bought a giant box of mixed-up puzzle pieces from your internet company—each piece is a tiny bit of information about what people do online, like which websites they visit or what they search for, but it's all jumbled and anonymous so you can't tell which pieces belong to which specific person.

title: The geometric "what comes next?" type of questions on IQ tests.
text: Think of these puzzles like a game where shapes change in a simple, repeating pattern, and you have to guess the next move—like noticing that every time you clap, you then stomp, so after a stomp, you know a clap comes next.

title: What does this ISP selling browser history mean for me?
text: Think of your internet history like a list of all the places you visit in a big city, and your internet company (the ISP) is like the bus driver who takes you there. A new rule says the bus driver is now allowed to make copies of everyone's list and sell those copies to shops that want to advertise to you. This means you might start seeing more ads that feel very personal, like for a toy you looked up just once or a pizza place near your house. It also means companies you don't know could learn a lot about your habits. To keep your list more private, you can use special tools like a VPN (which is like taking a secret tunnel instead of the bus) or use websites that start with "https://" (which is like sending a sealed letter instead of a postcard).

title: Why does stretching feel so much better right before you go to sleep and right after you wake up?
text: Stretching feels extra good at bedtime and in the morning because your body has been still for a long time. When you sleep, your muscles relax and get a little stiff, so a morning stretch wakes them up by sending more blood to them, which feels like a nice, warm wake-up call. At night, your body is winding down and full of tension from the day, so stretching helps push that tightness out, telling your muscles it's time to relax and get ready for sleep.

title: How is it that the distance between Earth and the moon can supposedly fit all of the planets, but pictures show the moon relatively close to Earth?
text: Imagine you have a big ball for Earth and a smaller ball for the moon, and if you lined up all the other planet balls in between, they would just fit—that’s true, but only if you squish the planets together without any space around them. In real life, the moon is actually very far from Earth, about 30 Earths apart, but it looks close in pictures because space is so huge that even that big distance looks small when you see both in the same photo.

title: How do popular YouTubers make money?
text: Popular YouTubers make money in a few main ways, like getting paid for ads that play before or during their videos, getting sponsors to pay them to talk about products, selling their own merchandise like t-shirts, and sometimes getting fans to support them directly through memberships or tips.

title: Why do hot drinks feel even more hot when you're drinking through a straw?
text: When you drink a hot drink through a straw, the hot liquid goes straight to the back of your mouth where it's extra sensitive, instead of first touching your cooler lips or the front of your tongue, so it feels hotter right away.

title: Patreon?
text: Patreon is like a special piggy bank for people who make cool things you like, such as videos, music, or art. Instead of buying each thing separately, you put a little money into their piggy bank every month, and in return, they share their new creations with you first and sometimes give you extra special treats.

title: How/Why are queen insects such as ants and wasps so much bigger than the normal ones. Are they a different species or just lucky with genes?
text: Queen insects are bigger because they get special food when they're young, like a super-powered baby food that helps them grow into adults that can lay lots of eggs, and they also have different genes that tell their bodies to become queens instead of regular workers.

title: What would happen if you introduced a flame to a gas giant planet?
text: If you tried to light a gas giant like Jupiter with a match, it wouldn't catch fire like a balloon full of gas because most of the planet is made of hydrogen, and fire needs oxygen to burn—and there's almost no oxygen in a gas giant. Instead, if you could get deep inside where the pressure and heat are enormous, the hydrogen would already be acting more like a hot, thick liquid or metal, and adding a tiny flame would be like trying to light a campfire in the middle of a volcano: it wouldn't really do anything noticeable at all.

title: Is electricity affected by gravity?
text: Yes, electricity is affected by gravity, but not in a way you'd easily notice—imagine gravity as a gentle slope that everything slides down, even light and electricity, but for electricity it's such a tiny slide that you need super-sensitive tools to see it.

title: How am I able to play complex chords and intricate riffs on guitar with my non-dominant hand, yet can't even write my name with it properly?
text: Think of your hands like two different workers at a job. Your dominant hand, the one you write with, is like a master artist who has practiced drawing tiny, detailed pictures for years. Your other hand, on the guitar, is more like a strong, clever machine that has practiced doing a few very specific jobs over and over—like pressing buttons (the frets) in exact patterns. You trained that machine-hand just for guitar, so it’s great at that one task, but it never learned how to draw the delicate, wobbly lines of your name.

title: What was so bad about the European Union that UK voted to get out?
text: Imagine the European Union is like a big club that many countries in Europe joined to make it easier to trade toys and cookies, and to agree on rules like how to keep playgrounds safe. Some people in the UK felt that being in this club meant they had to follow too many rules made by the club leaders, pay a lot of membership fees, and let many people from other club countries come live and work in the UK, which they worried made it harder to find jobs and crowded schools and hospitals. So, they voted to leave the club, hoping they could make their own rules, control their borders better, and save money, even though it might make trading toys and cookies a bit more complicated.

title: how does dust form? And what generates the biggest amount of dust?
text: Dust is mostly made of tiny bits of things that have broken apart or fallen off. It comes from things like your own skin, little flakes from clothes and carpets, dirt from outside that gets tracked in, and even tiny pieces of plants and bugs. The biggest amount of dust usually comes from outside, especially from soil and dirt that gets blown around by the wind.

title: What is muscle memory?
text: Muscle memory is like when you learn to do something with your body so many times that your brain and muscles remember how to do it all by themselves, like riding a bike or tying your shoes, so you don't have to think about each step anymore.

title: how come we can see fog in the distance but not directly in front of us?
text: Think of fog like a huge crowd of tiny water droplets floating in the air—when you look through it, you’re looking at a bunch of them together. Up close, there aren’t enough droplets between your eyes and the fog to block your view, so it seems clear. But when you look far away, your sight has to pass through many, many more droplets, and all together they scatter enough light to look like a visible white cloud.

title: Why do we laugh? Specifically why do we have a physical reaction, such as chest heaving, when we laugh rather than just "feeling" happy?
text: We laugh because our brain gets a surprise, like a tickle or a silly joke, and it sends a message to our body to let out happy energy. The chest heaving and loud sounds happen because laughing makes us breathe in and out really fast, almost like a fun exercise for our belly and lungs, which helps share our good feelings with others and makes the happiness feel even bigger.

title: Why does the US model of the Samsung Galaxy S8 have a different processor than the global model?
text: The US model of the Samsung Galaxy S8 uses a different processor mainly because of cell phone networks. In the US, the big networks like Verizon and AT&T use a special kind of technology that the global processor doesn't work with very well. So, Samsung uses a different processor in the US that's better at talking to those US networks, making sure your phone gets good service for calls and internet. It's like having two different kinds of walkie-talkies—if you want to talk to a specific group, you need to use the walkie-talkie that works on their channel.

title: With 125 million people working in the USA, why do we get huge amounts of national news coverage concerning a factory that will provide 130 jobs?
text: Imagine the whole country is a giant playground, and everyone has a job to do, like being on the swing team or the slide team. When a brand new, really cool swing set gets built that lets 130 more kids play, it's a big deal because it shows that the playground is growing and getting better, and it gives hope that more new swing sets might be built for even more kids in the future.

title: What's the difference between what congress did yesterday to sell your browser history and what yahoo/google/Facebook was already doing?
text: Congress didn't actually pass a law to sell your browser history—instead, they voted to stop a new rule from taking effect that would have required internet service providers (like Comcast or Verizon) to ask your permission before sharing your private information, while companies like Google and Facebook already collect your information when you use their websites or apps, but they mostly do it under their own rules where you agree to it when you sign up, so the big difference is that now your internet company has fewer restrictions on what they can do with your data compared to websites you visit.

title: How come senators and congressmen in the US can accept donations from corporations? Wouldn't this be directly against the interest of people?
text:
Think of elections like a big, expensive game where you need lots of money to tell people about yourself—like buying ads, traveling, and having a team to help. Politicians are allowed to accept donations from companies, but there are rules: the money can't go straight into their pocket for personal things like a new car. Instead, it goes into a special campaign account to help them run for office.

The tricky part is that some people worry this is like a company buying a favor, since the politician might feel like they should help that company later with a new law. To try and stop this, there are rules about how much money anyone—including a company—can give, and everyone has to say who gave them money so it's not a secret. But many people still think it's a problem because companies with a lot of money can have a louder voice than regular people, which can make it feel like the game isn't fair for everyone.

title: What happens to calories when they are "burned"?
text: Think of calories like tiny pieces of food energy inside your body. When you run, jump, or even just breathe, your body needs energy to work, just like a toy car needs batteries. To get that energy, your body "burns" the calories. It doesn't use fire, but it mixes the calories with the air you breathe in a special way inside your cells. This process turns the food energy into the energy you use to move and think, and it also makes heat to keep you warm and waste products (like carbon dioxide) that you breathe out. So, the calories don't disappear—they change into energy and heat for your body to use.

title: If it only cost 8m to buy out our senators for the ISP deal, why can't we raise that money and lobby ourselves?
text: That's a great question! Think of it like this: even if you and your friends saved up enough money to buy the same toy as the big kid, the store might still only listen to the big kid because he buys toys every week and promises to buy even more later. In the same way, the big internet companies don't just give money once—they promise senators jobs, fancy trips, and lots more money over many years, so the senators keep listening to them instead of just us.

title: How does an American senator/representative get lobbied to enact a law? Is it really just as easy as "I'll donate to your campaign if you make a bill that allows selling internet history"?
text: It's not usually that simple and direct, like a straight-up trade, because that would be illegal bribery. Instead, think of it like making a new friend who really wants you to like their favorite toy. The lobbyist (who works for a company or group) starts by giving the senator helpful information, explaining why their idea for a law is good for jobs or for people in the state. They might also promise to help the senator by telling their members to vote for them. The campaign donation is more like a gift that says, "I'm your friend and I support you," hoping that when it's time to decide about the toy—or the law—the senator remembers their friendly helper and agrees with them. So it's a longer game of building a relationship, not just a quick deal.

title: Is there a proven limit to computation power?
text: Think of a computer like a super-fast puzzle solver—it can solve many puzzles, but some puzzles are so tricky that even the fastest computer would take longer than the age of the universe to finish them. Scientists have found that there are certain problems that are just too hard for any computer, no matter how powerful, to solve quickly. So yes, there are limits to what even the best computer can do, kind of like how even the fastest runner can't run faster than the speed of light.

title: Why is nutrition so complex?
text: Nutrition seems complex because our bodies are like tiny, busy cities that need lots of different workers—like vitamins, minerals, and other nutrients—to keep everything running smoothly, and figuring out exactly how much of each "worker" we need from our food can be tricky since every person's body is a little different.

title: How is it ensured that pills/tablets contain the exact amount of multiple ingredients ?
text: Pills are made like tiny, careful recipes where machines measure and mix the ingredients just like a baker measures flour and sugar, but with super-precise scales and mixers to make sure every single pill gets the exact same amount of each ingredient.

title: why do we forget things we just read?
text: Imagine your brain is like a toy box with only so much room inside—when you learn something new, like a fact from a book, it’s like putting a new toy in the box, but if you don’t play with that toy often, it might get buried under other toys and be harder to find later, so you forget it.

title: why do we have intrusive thoughts?
text: Intrusive thoughts are like your brain's pop-up ads that you didn't ask for—they're weird, sudden ideas or images that pop into your head, like thinking about yelling in a quiet place or jumping when you're somewhere high. Everyone gets them sometimes. They happen because your brain is always busy sorting through thoughts to keep you safe and help you make decisions, and sometimes it accidentally brings up a scary or silly one just to check if it's important. It's usually your brain's way of reminding you what *not* to do, and most of the time, you can just notice the thought and let it float away like a cloud.

title: Why is Scotland having a second referendum vote? Why does it seem like some people view the possibility of Scottish independence as a bad thing, rather than a good thing?
text: Scotland is having another vote because some people there want to be their own country, separate from the United Kingdom, and they feel that things have changed a lot since the last vote in 2014. Some people think independence is a good idea because Scotland could make all its own decisions about things like money and laws, but others think it's a bad idea because it might make things more expensive and complicated, like sharing money or keeping friends with the rest of the UK.

title: What is the logical argument behind the Bill allowing ISP'S to sell customer data?
text: Imagine your internet company is like a mailman who sees all the letters you send and receive; a new rule says that mailman is allowed to tell other companies what you're interested in, and the main argument is that it helps those other companies show you ads for things you might actually want to buy.

title: Why is it easy to tear paper in half but not to pull it apart?
text: Imagine paper is made of lots of tiny fibers that are all lined up in rows, like a handful of straws bundled together—when you tear it, you’re pulling just a few of those straws at a time, and they start to split apart one by one, which doesn’t take much effort. But if you try to pull the whole paper apart from both ends, you’re tugging on all the straws at once, and they work together to hold on tight, making it much harder to break.

title: What happens to the old pavement when a road gets repaved?
text: When a road gets repaved, the old pavement isn't just buried under the new stuff—first, big machines with spinning teeth chew up the top layer of the old, cracked road, breaking it into small chunks. Those chunks are then scooped up and taken to a special place where they can be crushed into even smaller pieces and recycled to help build new roads, parking lots, or even the base for playgrounds.

title: Why do we compare foot numbness or that fuzzy foot feeling with static on a tv channel?
text: We compare that fuzzy foot feeling to static on a TV because both happen when the normal signals get mixed up and scrambled—your foot’s “TV channel” isn’t getting a clear picture from your brain, so all you feel is a confusing buzz.

title: why is it easier to drag something heavy than it is to lift it?
text: Imagine you're trying to move a big, heavy box. When you lift it, you have to fight against the whole force of gravity pulling it straight down. But when you drag it, you're mostly just fighting against the roughness of the floor, like little bumps and sticky spots that try to hold it back. It’s like the difference between picking up a whole puppy versus just sliding its food bowl across the kitchen floor—sliding is much easier because gravity isn’t pulling down on it as much.

title: What is an API?
text: Think of an API like a waiter in a restaurant. You, the customer, sit at the table with a menu of choices, and the kitchen is the part of the company that makes the food. You can't just go into the kitchen and start cooking—you need someone to take your order and bring your food back. The waiter is the messenger that takes your request to the kitchen and then delivers the food to you. In the same way, an API is a messenger that takes your request (like wanting to see a weather forecast on your phone) to a system (like a big weather computer), gets the information, and brings it back to your app so you can see it.

title: How is it that we can get the molecular composition of substances on planets a million miles away, but the Coca-Cola recipe is still a secret?
text: We can figure out what planets are made of by looking at the light they give off or reflect, kind of like how a prism splits sunlight into a rainbow—different substances leave unique fingerprints in that rainbow of light. The Coca-Cola recipe, on the other hand, is a secret kept in a vault because it’s a specific mix of common ingredients that’s very hard to guess just by tasting it, and the company works hard to keep it hidden.

title: What IS Autism??
text: Autism is like having a different operating system in your brain than most other people. It means your brain takes in information from the world—like sounds, lights, and social cues—in its own unique way. This can make some things, like loud noises or big crowds, feel really overwhelming, but it can also make you incredibly focused and an expert on things you love, like dinosaurs or train schedules. Just like computers with different systems can all do amazing things, people with autism have wonderful strengths and see the world in a special way.

title: How do they recyle plastic when it is toxic to breathe when burned?
text: When plastic gets recycled, they don't burn it like trash—instead, they sort it, wash it, chop it into tiny pieces, and melt it down to make new things, which is much safer and doesn't create the toxic smoke that burning plastic does.

title: what's the difference between visa, MasterCard, and all the other cards?
text: Think of your money like a toy you want to buy from a store, but the store only takes special notes from your parents. Visa and MasterCard are like two different companies that make those special notes. They don't actually give you the money—that comes from your piggy bank (your bank account). Their job is to run really fast between the store and your piggy bank to tell everyone it's okay to trade the toy for your money. Other cards, like American Express or Discover, are just other companies that do the same running-around job, but they sometimes have different stores that like them best or different rules for how you pay them back.

title: How are polls of around 1500 people regarding political opinions kept as accurate as possible? It seems that it isn't a high enough sample to get an accurate average.
text: Imagine you have a huge jar filled with millions of different colored marbles, and you want to know what percent are red without counting every single one. If you stir the jar really well and then pull out a handful of marbles, the colors in your hand will probably match the whole jar pretty closely—as long as you grabbed them randomly and your handful is big enough. Polls work the same way: they carefully choose about 1,500 people to represent the whole country, making sure the group matches the population in terms of age, where they live, and other important traits. This small, well-mixed sample is surprisingly accurate because math shows that once you have a certain number of people, adding more doesn’t improve accuracy much, just like how a second handful of marbles mostly tells you what you already learned from the first.

title: What information, explicitly, can now be sold by ISPs? It looks like the new law was replacing rules that had not yet gone into affect, so how is this any different than how the internet was 4 years ago? Could our data have been sold then before the rules that were voted on in Oct 2016?
text:
Think of your internet provider like the company that delivers your mail. For a while, there were brand new rules being made that said the mail carrier wasn't allowed to peek at your letters, make a list of what you're buying and who you're writing to, and then sell that list to other companies. But before those new rules could even start, Congress decided to throw them away.

So, right now, it's exactly the same as it was four years ago. Back then, and again now, your internet provider *could* collect and sell a lot of information about you, like a list of every website you visit, every app you use on your phone, and where you are when you use them. They could sell that to advertisers who want to show you very specific ads. The main difference is that for a few months, we thought those new privacy rules were going to protect us, but now we know they won't be starting after all.

title: What is the difference between the old USB and USB C?
text: Think of the old USB like a puzzle piece that only fits one way, and you often have to flip it over a few times to get it right—it’s a bit slow for moving things like movies. USB-C is like a super puzzle piece that fits no matter which way you plug it in, and it’s much faster, so it can move big things like movies in a snap, plus it can even charge your laptop or tablet much quicker.

title: Why do we feel embarrassed for others who have nothing to do with us?
text: We feel embarrassed for others because our brains are really good at imagining how we would feel in their situation, almost like we’re putting ourselves in their shoes without even trying.

title: computers today have a CPU and a GPU. They use the GPU to do calculation because they say GPUs are much faster, so why in the hell they don't make CPUs as faster as GPUs and they can still have a GPU and make the whole thing faster as hell?
text: Think of a CPU like a really smart chef who can do any recipe step-by-step, while a GPU is like having a hundred helpers who only know how to chop vegetables. The GPU is faster at chopping because all the helpers work at once, but the chef is still needed to decide what to cook and do the tricky parts. If you tried to make the chef have a hundred hands like the helpers, he’d get too big, complicated, and expensive, and he’d still be slower at just chopping because all those extra hands would get in the way of his thinking. So computers use both: the smart chef (CPU) to run the show and the many helpers (GPU) to do simple jobs over and over really fast.

title: Why is a massive company donating to politicians not consider bribing?
text:
Imagine you and your friends are deciding what game to play, and one friend really wants everyone to play their favorite game, so they offer to share their special snacks with everyone if they agree. That's a bit like a bribe—it's a direct trade: snacks for getting your way right now.

A big company giving money to a politician is more like them saying, "I really like the games you pick and the way you play, so here's some money to help you keep being the game-chooser." The rules say they can't give money to get a specific, immediate favor, like passing one exact law just for them. Instead, the money is supposed to be to help politicians they generally agree with get elected so they can make rules the company likes. The tricky part is that everyone knows the company hopes those politicians will remember the help later, which is why it feels like a bribe even though the law calls it a donation and has special rules for it.

title: Why are there words that don't sound right if you say them over and over?
text: When you say a word over and over, your brain gets used to the sounds and starts to focus on them too much, making the word feel strange and unfamiliar, almost like it’s not a real word anymore.

title: How do our eyes stay shut whilst we sleep?
text: Our eyes stay shut while we sleep because a tiny part of your brain sends a message to the muscles around your eyes, telling them to relax and close your eyelids, like a soft curtain, to keep out light and protect your eyes so they can rest just like the rest of your body.

title: Were T-rex's arms functional? If so, what were they useful for?
text: Yes, T-rex's arms were functional, and they were useful for helping it get up from the ground after resting, and they might have also been used to hold onto prey tightly while the T-rex used its huge, powerful jaws to take a bite.

title: Are cellphones susceptible to the same viruses PC and Mac are?
text: Yes, but not as often! Think of your phone like a smaller, simpler computer that mostly stays in its own little playground—it has strong fences (security) and doesn't let in as many strange programs. Computers are like big, open parks where more people can visit and sometimes leave messy things (viruses) behind. So while phones can get sick with viruses too, especially if you download apps from strange places, it happens much less than with computers.

title: How does it work out that blue and red are both primary colors of light and pigment but yellow is the third primary pigment color and green is the third primary color of light?
text: Think of light like mixing flashlights and paint like mixing clay. With light, you start with red, green, and blue flashlights—shine them all together and you get white light, and mixing red and green makes yellow. With paint, the colors work by *absorbing* light instead. Your starting paints are cyan (a light blue), magenta (a bright pink), and yellow. Mixing yellow and cyan paint makes green because together they absorb all light except green. So even though we often say "red, blue, and yellow" for paint, the true primary pigments are actually cyan, magenta, and yellow, and green isn't a starting color—it's made by mixing.

title: What's physically going on when your eye transitions from focusing on something far away to something closer?
text: Think of your eye like a tiny camera with a stretchy lens inside. When you look at something far away, the lens stays relaxed and flat, but when you look at something close, a little muscle squeezes to make the lens fatter and rounder so it can bend the light just right to make a clear picture on the back of your eye.

title: How do free tax-preparation websites make money?
text: Free tax-preparation websites make money by offering you a free basic version, but then they often charge you for extra things like if you have more complicated taxes, need to file state taxes, or want extra help—and sometimes they also make money by suggesting financial products you might buy, like a loan if you're getting a tax refund.

title: Why do airplanes board passengers from front to back? Seems like people wouldn't get in each other's way so much if they did back to front.
text: Airplanes board from front to back because it's simpler for the airline, even if it seems slower. Think of it like putting groceries in a bag—if you put the heavy cans in first (the people in the back seats), the bread at the top (the front seats) might get squished. By filling the front first, the flight attendants can help people find their seats without everyone squeezing past each other in a tiny aisle, and it also helps make sure the plane is balanced properly for takeoff. Some airlines do try faster ways, like boarding window seats first, but the front-to-back method is the easiest to organize when you have a lot of people and a tight schedule.

title: Why do some YouTube videos that show episodes of TV shows have unrelated borders in them that take up a third of the screen?
text: That's because the people who uploaded those videos are trying to trick YouTube's computer police! YouTube has special programs that automatically check if a video is a copy of a TV show or movie, which isn't allowed. To hide from those programs, the uploaders will put big, weird borders or spin the video sideways, making it look different. They hope the computer will think it's a new, silly video instead of recognizing the TV show inside. It doesn't really work well for long, and the videos usually get taken down anyway.

title: What was the starting point that lead to a successful rocket launch into space? How does it not take a million incremental tests to get to the end goal?
text: Think of building a rocket like learning to ride a bike—you don’t start by trying to ride down a huge hill right away. First, you learn about balance on a safe, flat path, and you might even use training wheels. For rockets, scientists and engineers start with a lot of math and small models on computers to figure out how things should work. Then they test parts separately, like the engines and fuel tanks, before putting everything together. They also learn from every test, even the failures, so each new rocket is smarter and safer. It’s like having a really good instruction manual from all the smart people who tried before, so you don’t have to start from scratch every time.

title: How does autorotation allow hellicopters to land safely?
text: Imagine a helicopter's spinning blades are like a big, flat playground slide; if the engine stops, the helicopter can tilt the slide so air rushes up through it as it falls, which keeps the blades spinning and lets the pilot steer and slow down for a safe landing, just like a maple seed twirling to the ground.

title: Why does our nose run when we cry?
text: When you cry, your tears don't just come out of your eyes—some of them drain into tiny tubes in the corners of your eyes that lead to the inside of your nose. Your nose makes extra mucus (the wet, sticky stuff) to mix with those tears, and that makes your nose feel runny, just like when you have a cold.

title: Why is sitting considered bad for you as opposed to squatting?
text: Think of your body like a squishy toy that's happiest when it's moving around. Sitting in a chair for a long time is like squishing the toy into one shape and leaving it there—it can get stiff and the springs inside can get weak. Squatting is more like a gentle, active stretch for your whole body; it keeps your muscles working and your bones and joints in a strong, natural position, just like how people used to rest before chairs were invented. So, sitting too much can make your body tired and weak, while squatting helps keep it springy and strong.

title: Who, whom, whoever, whomever, and whomsoever. How do these work?
text: Think of "who" and "whoever" as the doers of an action, like the subject of a sentence, and "whom" and "whomever" as the receivers of an action, like the object. A simple trick is to try answering the question with "he" or "him." If "he" fits, use "who"; if "him" fits, use "whom." For example, "Who/whom ate the cookie?" (He ate it, so "who" is correct). "Who/whom did you see?" (You saw him, so "whom" is correct). "Whoever" and "whomever" work the same way but are used for more open-ended situations, like "Give it to whoever/whomever wants it" (He wants it, so "whoever"). "Whomsoever" is just a very formal version of "whomever" that you'll rarely need. Most people just use "who" and "whoever" all the time in everyday talking, and that's perfectly okay.

title: why does anaesthetic make you say weird things when you wake up?
text: Anesthesia is like a sleepy medicine that turns off the part of your brain that controls your thoughts and filters what you say, so when you start waking up, that filter is still turned off and your sleepy brain just says whatever silly or secret thing pops into your head before the thinking part catches up.

title: Why does turning on lights / flickering lights make sound? Do light make sound?
text: Lights themselves don't make sound, but the things we use to create light often do! When you flip a switch, electricity rushes through the wires to the light bulb, and that sudden zap can cause tiny parts inside the switch or the bulb to vibrate very quickly—like a really fast drumbeat—and our ears hear those vibrations as a click or a buzz.

title: When they do the first human head transplant, is the person in the head getting a new body or is the human in the body getting a new head?
text: That's a tricky question because it's really about where we think "you" live in your body. Most scientists and doctors believe that "you" — your thoughts, memories, and personality — are all in your brain, which is inside your head. So if a head transplant ever happened, the person whose head is being moved would be getting a whole new body, while the body would be getting a new head (and a whole new person attached to it). It would be like moving the driver from a broken car into a new car — the driver is still the same person, just with a different vehicle.

title: Why do we have a "right" and a "left" foot?
text: We have a right and a left foot because our bodies are mostly symmetrical, which means the two sides are like mirror images, and this helps us walk and balance better.

title: What is the mean center of population?
text: Imagine all the people in a country are standing outside on a giant flat map, and you want to find the exact spot where you could perfectly balance that map on the tip of your finger—that spot is called the mean center of population.

title: How can dolphins hold their breath for so long, while other mammals need to breathe constantly?
text: Dolphins can hold their breath for a long time because their bodies are built like super swimmers—they store extra oxygen in their muscles, slow their heartbeat to save air when they dive, and have a special reflex that stops them from breathing in water by accident.

title: Why does cold water taste better than room temperature water?
text: Cold water tastes better because our taste buds are more sensitive when they're cool, making the water seem crisper and more refreshing, while warmer water can bring out flavors that might seem a bit flat or stale.

title: How did we first find out about the difference in gravity in space?
text: We first learned about the difference in gravity in space by noticing that things don't fall the same way everywhere on Earth—like how a pendulum clock would run a tiny bit slower near the equator than at the poles—and then by sending rockets and satellites up high. When objects like the Moon orbit Earth, they are actually falling toward us but moving sideways so fast that they keep missing, and that happens because gravity gets weaker the farther away you go. Scientists like Isaac Newton figured out the rules for this, and later, astronauts floating in the International Space Station showed us that even though they look weightless, Earth's gravity is still pulling on them—they're just in constant freefall around the planet, which feels like zero gravity.

title: Why is it ok to eat duck rare, but not chicken?
text: Duck is okay to eat rare because its meat is denser and has less of the harmful bacteria that chickens often carry, so cooking it all the way through isn't as necessary to keep you safe.

title: What who loses money on unsold food, the supermarket or the food manufacturer?
text: Usually it's the supermarket that loses money on unsold food, because they already bought it from the manufacturer, so it's like they bought a toy that nobody ended up buying from them.

title: How does splitting an atom harness so much power?
text: Think of an atom like a tiny, super-tightly packed bundle of energy held together with invisible glue. When you split it, that bundle breaks open and all the stored-up energy inside bursts out at once—like popping a balloon that’s been squeezed really, really hard, but with millions of times more force.

title: Why do some things melt while others burn?
text: Think of melting like ice cream turning into a puddle on a hot day—it’s just changing from a solid to a liquid, but it’s still the same stuff. Burning is different: it’s like when you put a piece of paper in a fire and it turns into smoke and ash, which is completely new stuff. Some things, like metal or ice, just get softer and melt when they get hot. Other things, like wood or leaves, catch fire because the heat makes them mix with the air in a way that creates flames and changes them forever.

title: How does Bear Grylls avoid severe gastro-intestinal infection after drinking water, squeezed out of elephant feces in hot African climate?
text: Bear Grylls avoids getting sick from dirty water like elephant poop water because he doesn't actually drink it for real on the show—the risky parts are filmed under very careful supervision, and he gets immediate medical help afterwards, including strong medicine that kills the germs that would normally make him very sick.

title: How can Eris be 27% more massive than Pluto, yet Pluto have a larger volume?
text: Think of Eris and Pluto like two balls of clay—Eris is made of heavier, denser clay packed tightly together, so it's heavier even though it's a bit smaller, while Pluto is made of lighter, fluffier clay that takes up more space, making it bigger in size but not as heavy.

title: why is the ¢50 dollar coin so uncommon?
text: The 50¢ coin is uncommon because people don't use it very often—it's big and heavy, so it's not as handy as a quarter, and most vending machines and parking meters aren't even designed to take it, so it just ends up sitting in jars or drawers instead of being passed around.

title: Why does having a strong core help with exercises like pull ups?
text: Having a strong core is like having a tight, sturdy middle section in your body, and when you do a pull-up, it helps keep your legs from swinging around like a wobbly noodle so all your power can go straight into pulling yourself up.

title: How do anti-nausea patches administer medicine to the body?
text: Anti-nausea patches are like tiny medicine stickers you put behind your ear. They have special medicine soaked into the sticky part, and when you put the patch on your skin, the medicine slowly seeps through your skin, like a sponge dripping water, and goes into your blood. Your blood then carries the medicine around your body to help your stomach feel better without you having to swallow a pill.

title: Why do chickens have white meat and dark meat?
text: Chickens have white meat and dark meat because of how much they use their muscles. Chickens mostly walk around, so the muscles in their legs and thighs work a lot and need more oxygen, which makes them darker. Their wings and breasts aren't used as much for flying, so those muscles are lighter and become white meat.

title: What data can ISPs now sell?
text: Internet providers can now sell information about what you do online, like which websites you visit, what apps you use, and where you are when you use your phone, but they can't sell your name or address directly with that information.

title: Why the (0-1) infinite bigger than the (0,1,2,3,...) infinite?
text: Think of numbers between 0 and 1, like 0.1, 0.01, or 0.14159... — there are so many that you can't even list them in order like 1, 2, 3... because between any two you can always find another, making this infinity way bigger than the kind you can count.

title: Why are kiwi fruits and peaches hairy?
text: Kiwi fruits and peaches are hairy because their fuzzy skin helps protect them just like a cozy sweater! The tiny hairs keep bugs from wanting to eat them, help keep moisture inside so they don’t dry out, and even shield them from too much sun, which is why they grow this soft, furry coat to stay safe and healthy until they’re ready to be picked.

title: why can't you divide by zero?
text: Imagine you have a bunch of cookies and you want to share them equally with your friends—if you try to share them with zero friends, it doesn’t make sense because there’s no one to give them to, so you can’t figure out how many cookies each person gets.

title: Why does apple cider, unlike most fizzy drinks, always throth its way out of the bottle/can, no matter how carefully you move it?
text: Apple cider is made from apples, which have natural sugars that turn into a special kind of gas when they ferment, and this gas likes to stick to tiny bits of apple floating in the drink—so when you open the bottle, all those little bits give the gas an easy escape route, causing a bubbly explosion that’s much harder to control than in drinks like soda.

title: Why is the 'QWERTY' keyboard not arranged in alphabetical order?
text: The QWERTY keyboard was designed a long time ago for old typewriters, and if the keys were in alphabetical order, the metal arms with the letters would jam together when people typed too fast, so they mixed up the letters to slow typists down and keep the machines working.

title: Is quality of sleep affected by how you wake up?
text: Yes, the way you wake up can definitely affect how good your sleep feels! If you wake up naturally when your body is ready, you usually feel more rested and happy, but if a loud alarm suddenly jolts you awake, it can make you feel groggy and grumpy because it interrupts your deep sleep.

title: Why can humans draw near-perfect curves without thinking in one stroke, but when trying to recreate it at a slower pace and while thinking about it, they cannot?
text: Think of your brain like two friends: one is super fast and doesn't overthink, and the other is slow and careful. When you draw a curve quickly without thinking, you're using the fast friend who works on instinct, like catching a ball without looking—your hand just knows what to do. But when you go slow and think about it, the slow friend takes over, trying to control every tiny movement, which makes your hand shaky and unsure because it's not used to being micromanaged. So, sometimes trying too hard actually makes things harder!

title: Does running in the rain help you stay more dry, or does it not matter if the rate of rainfall is constant?
text:
If you run in the rain, you'll get less wet because you spend less time in the rain, so fewer raindrops hit you from above—but when you run, you also crash into more raindrops in front of you, kind of like running through a sprinkler.  
If the rain is falling straight down, running helps a lot because you get out of the rain faster.  
If the rain is coming at you sideways because of wind, then running might not help as much because you keep running into the side rain.  
So in most cases, running does help you stay a little more dry, especially if it’s not too windy.

title: Why do people's legs move in synchronization when walking next to each other?
text: When you walk next to someone, your legs often naturally match their steps because it feels more comfortable and helps you stay together, kind of like clapping to the same beat in a song—it just makes things easier and more fun.

title: How did Dolphins go from being land animals to water animals?
text: A long, long time ago, dolphins' great-great-great grandparents looked more like small, furry wolves that lived near the water and ate fish. They liked the water so much that over millions of years, their bodies slowly changed to make swimming easier: their front legs became flippers, their back legs disappeared, their tails got flat and strong for paddling, and their noses moved to the top of their heads so they could breathe without lifting their whole face out of the water. It was a very, very slow change, like a family getting better and better at swimming with each new generation, until they became the dolphins we know today.

title: What exactly is vantablack? How does it work?
text: Vantablack is a special kind of paint that is the darkest black ever made—it’s so dark that it looks like a hole or like something disappeared! It works because it’s made of millions of tiny, super thin tubes, like a microscopic forest of grass; when light hits it, instead of bouncing back to your eyes, it gets trapped between those tubes and turns into a tiny bit of heat, so almost no light comes back out, making it look incredibly black.

title: We download antivirus software on our laptops but not our phones, despite using our phones for the same sorta stuff. Is that cos our phones are already more secure? If so, why can't laptops be made as secure too? [Technology]
text: Phones are like toys that come in a locked box—they have built-in security that only lets you download apps from a safe store, and each app is kept in its own separate compartment so if one is bad it can't easily mess with the rest. Laptops are more like toolboxes that are open for you to add any tool from anywhere, which is handy but means bad tools can sneak in more easily, so we add antivirus software as an extra lock. Laptops could be made as secure as phones, but then they'd be less flexible for all the different programs people want to use, like for work or hobbies, so it's a trade-off between keeping things super safe and keeping them open and versatile.

title: Why do people say it is bad to skip breakfast?
text: People say it's bad to skip breakfast because your body is like a car that has been parked all night—it needs fuel in the morning to get going and have energy for the day ahead. Eating breakfast helps you think better at school or work, keeps you from getting too hungry and grumpy later, and can help you make healthier choices all day long.

title: Why did contact with the Vikings not have the same effect on Native American population that contact with Europeans at a later date did?
text: Think of it like this: the Vikings came over for a quick visit, like kids running into a neighbor's yard, grabbing a few things, and then running back home because they got into a fight. They only stayed in a few small spots for a short time, and there weren't very many of them, so they didn't share their germs much or try to take over the land. Later, when other Europeans came, it was like a huge moving truck and hundreds of people showing up to stay forever; they brought lots of germs that made the Native Americans very sick, and they also wanted to build their own towns and farms everywhere, which led to much bigger fights over the land.

title: How are we able to isolate the different instruments sounds or voices when listening to music?
text: When you listen to music, it's like hearing a big bowl of mixed-up fruit salad—your brain is really good at picking out the tastes of the different fruits, like strawberries or bananas, even though they're all mixed together. For music, each instrument or voice makes its own special sound pattern, like a unique musical fingerprint, and your ears and brain work together to notice these differences and follow each one, so you can hear the singer separately from the guitar or the drums.

title: Why all of sudden does an army of worms appear all over the ground when it's raining outside?
text: Worms live underground where it’s damp and safe, but when it rains a lot, the water fills up their tunnels and makes it hard for them to breathe, so they wiggle up to the surface to get some air. Also, the wet ground makes it easier for them to move without drying out, so you see them all over until the rain stops and they can go back home.

title: Why does the scent of garlic stick to your fingers so strongly?
text: Garlic has special smelly juice inside it that gets on your fingers when you touch it, and that juice is so tiny and sticky that it sneaks into the tiny holes in your skin and doesn’t want to come out, even when you wash with soap and water—it’s like it uses little hooks to hold on tight until your skin naturally wears away over time.

title: If a group of, say, children were raised alone in total silence, with no external exposure to language, would the children develop a language between them?
text: Yes, they would likely create their own way of communicating, and over time it could grow into a full language with its own rules, just like how all human languages started long ago.

title: Why is it easier to lift living beings of say, 20kgs, than an object of 20kgs?
text: Imagine your muscles are like a team of helpers that need to know exactly how to pick something up—living things like a wiggly dog or a person can help by adjusting their own weight and moving with you, making them feel lighter, while a stiff, heavy box just sits there and makes your helpers do all the work alone.

title: how do game developers determine the level of complexity and fidelity they can get in their engine from a hardware platform?
text: Game developers figure out how fancy they can make their game by doing a lot of testing, kind of like trying to see how many toys you can fit in your toy box without it overflowing. They look at the hardware (like the PlayStation, Xbox, or a computer) and think about the most important parts: the brain (CPU), the artist (GPU), and the memory (RAM). They make a simple version of their game first and keep adding details and effects until the hardware starts to slow down or get too hot, then they know they’ve hit the limit and they make the game just a little less complex so it runs smoothly for everyone.

title: Why do we get scared even when we know something is coming, like a bad scary movie or the damned toaster?
text: Even when we know something scary is coming, like a jump in a movie or a loud toaster pop, our body has a super-fast alarm system that works before our thinking brain can stop it. That alarm sends a rush of energy through us to get ready to run or fight, making our heart pound and muscles tense. So even though our smart brain knows it’s just a movie or toast, our body’s alarm has already been triggered because it’s trying to keep us safe from anything surprising or loud.

title: Are GMOs at all bad for us?
text: Think of GMOs like a superhero makeover for plants—scientists change a tiny part of the plant's instructions (its genes) to give it a special power, like growing bigger or staying safe from bugs. Just like how eating a regular carrot is good for you, eating a GMO carrot is also good for you, and after lots of checking by smart grown-ups, they are found to be just as safe to eat as other foods.

title: How does counting cards work?
text: Counting cards is like keeping a secret score in your head while playing a card game like blackjack, where you remember which high and low cards have already been played to guess if the next cards will be good or bad for you.

title: Why does baking/cooking something in the oven at 200°C for 15 min NOT have the same result as baking/cooking something at 3000°C for 1 min?
text: Imagine your food is like a snowman you want to melt just a little to make it tasty. If you use a warm oven, it’s like a sunny day that slowly melts the snowman evenly so it turns into a nice puddle. If you use an extremely hot oven, it’s like holding a giant firework right next to the snowman—it would instantly turn to steam and maybe even catch fire, leaving you with a burnt mess instead of a tasty treat. Cooking needs time for heat to travel inside the food gently, and too much heat too fast just burns the outside while the inside stays cold.

title: What actually happens to our skin when we apply lotion? How deep does the lotion go?
text: Think of your skin like a brick wall that's a little bit dry and cracked—lotion is like a gentle rain that helps fill in those cracks and adds a thin, slippery layer on top to keep moisture from escaping, but it doesn't soak all the way through to the inside.

title: Can the economy expand even if the unemployment rate also increases? If not, why?
text: Yes, the economy can grow even when the unemployment rate goes up, and it's a bit like a classroom where the teacher is handing out more cookies (that's the economy growing) but also inviting more new kids to join the class (that's more people looking for jobs). Sometimes the new kids are still finding their seats and haven't gotten a cookie yet, so even though there are more cookies overall, there are also more kids waiting to get one. In the real world, this can happen when lots of people start looking for work at the same time, or when businesses use machines to make more stuff with fewer workers, so the economy gets bigger but not everyone has a job right away.

title: Why is everyone so angry about the Senate passing the resolution to let ISPs sell our internet history now, rather than years ago?
text: Think of it like this: imagine a rule was made a few years ago that said your parents couldn't look at your diary without asking you first. Now, some people in charge just voted to get rid of that rule, so your parents could read it anytime. Even though the rule was new, you got used to having your privacy, so it feels extra scary and unfair to have it taken away right now.

title: what would happen globally if every human disappeared?
text: If every human suddenly disappeared, the world would slowly start to take over our stuff. First, the lights in cities would go out in a few hours as power plants ran out of fuel, and pets like dogs and cats would have to find their own food. Over weeks, animals would wander into towns, and plants would begin growing through cracks in roads and sidewalks. After a few years, houses and buildings would start to fall apart without people to fix them, and forests and wildlife would spread into empty neighborhoods. In a few hundred years, most cities would look like overgrown forests, with only the strongest things, like stone monuments or metal bridges, still standing, and nature would be back in charge.

title: How active is our brain during a coma?
text: Think of your brain like a busy office building where everyone has a job to do, like talking, moving, and thinking. When someone is in a coma, it's like most of the workers have gone home, but the lights are still on and a few important people are still there keeping the building running—like the janitor and the security guard. So the brain is still active doing basic jobs like breathing and keeping the heart beating, but it's not doing the big, busy tasks that make a person awake and aware.

title: Why aren't there any technical (vocational) schools in America?
text: That's a great question, but it's actually not quite right—there *are* technical and vocational schools in America! They're just often called by different names, like career and technical education (CTE) programs, trade schools, or they are special programs inside regular high schools or community colleges. Sometimes they aren't as talked about as going to a big university, but they are definitely there, teaching skills like fixing cars, building houses, cooking, healthcare jobs, and working with computers.

title: How can bacteria/fungus live in an aircraft fuel tank?
text: Think of airplane fuel like a special juice that the plane drinks to fly, and even though it seems like nothing could live in there, tiny germs called bacteria and fungus can sneak in with tiny water droplets that get into the tank. These germs are super tough and can eat tiny bits of the fuel itself, kind of like how you might snack on crumbs, and they can build slimy homes in the tank where the fuel and water mix together.

title: why does the death penalty take so long to administer?
text: Imagine you're playing a game where the punishment for breaking a very, very serious rule is that you have to leave and never come back—it's a really big deal. Because it's so big and final, everyone wants to be absolutely, positively sure they got the right person and that the rule was really broken fairly. So, the grown-ups check the rules over and over, look at all the evidence again, and let other grown-ups double-check their work. This checking takes a very long time, but it's to make sure a terrible mistake isn't made, since once the punishment happens, it can't be undone.

title: Why are bus steering wheels almost parallel to the ground, whereas car steering wheels are almost perpendicular to the ground?
text: Bus steering wheels are flat like a dinner plate because bus drivers sit up high and need to steer with big, sweeping turns of their arms without the wheel getting in the way, while car steering wheels are tilted like a bicycle wheel because car drivers sit lower and closer, making it easier to turn the wheel quickly with smaller movements.

title: What's the difference between gardening and farming?
text: Gardening is like having a small, personal playground for plants where you grow just enough flowers, vegetables, or herbs for yourself and your family, often in a backyard or pots. Farming is much bigger, like running a plant factory that grows huge amounts of food or materials to sell to lots of people, using large fields and big machines to help.

title: Why do we get restless when excited?
text: When you get excited, your body is like a puppy that hears the word "walk" — it gets a burst of energy and wants to move right away! This happens because your brain sends out special chemicals that make your heart beat faster and your muscles feel ready to go, so all that happy energy has to come out somehow, like wiggling, bouncing, or talking really fast.

title: What is a project scope?
text: Imagine you're building a big Lego castle. The project scope is like the plan you make with your friend before you start. It says exactly what you're going to build—like four towers, a wall, and a drawbridge—and also what you're *not* going to build, like no spaceship parts and no swimming pool. It helps everyone know what to expect so you don't end up arguing or running out of bricks.

title: US citzens, what happens If someone commits a crime in a state and runs to another state that what he has done is not ilegal?
text: If someone commits a crime in one state and runs to another state where that same act isn't illegal, they can still be caught and sent back to the first state to face charges because of a rule called the Full Faith and Credit Clause in the U.S. Constitution. This means states must respect each other's laws, so the state where the crime happened can ask the other state to return the person, which is called extradition.

title: When someone is hurt, what does "sent into shock" actually mean?
text: When someone gets hurt really badly, their body gets super confused and tries to protect itself by doing strange things—that's called shock. It's like your body's emergency system gets mixed up and sends all the blood to the most important parts, like your heart and brain, and away from your arms and legs. This can make the person feel very cold, dizzy, sweaty, and look very pale, almost like a scared ghost, because their body isn't working the right way anymore and needs help from a doctor fast.

title: Can the earth begin to weigh too much?
text: No, the Earth can't get too heavy because it's like a giant space rock that doesn't eat or collect extra stuff—almost all the new weight it ever gets is just tiny space dust, which is way too little to ever make it feel "too full."

title: How to fake number apps (such as Phoner, Burner, etc) work?
text: Think of these apps like a digital disguise for your phone number—they give you a second phone number that works on your phone without needing a second phone, so you can call, text, and get voicemails without giving out your real number, just like putting on a mask for a costume party.

title: How is SpaceX's successful reusable rocket landing more significant than the space shuttle program?
text: Think of the space shuttle like a big airplane that could come back to Earth and land on a runway, which was amazing, but it was also incredibly expensive and time-consuming to fix up and fly again—like having to rebuild the airplane after every trip. SpaceX’s reusable rocket is more like a regular airplane in a simpler way: it takes off, comes back, lands standing up, and after a quick check and refuel, it can fly again very soon, making it much cheaper and faster. This means going to space could become as common as flying on an airplane, opening up space for more people and bigger adventures.

title: Watching COPS and wondering why radios always sound so scratchy/crackly? Is it possible to get it as clear as the sound we get when talking through phones?
text: Radios sound scratchy because they send your voice through the air like a tiny invisible ball that can get bumped by buildings, weather, and other signals, which adds all that noise; phones sound clear because they send your voice through a protected wire or a very advanced digital signal that cleans it up, and while modern radios can be much clearer, they often prioritize reaching far distances over perfect sound.

title: how does overclocking a computer work?
text: Overclocking a computer is like telling a runner to go faster than they're supposed to—you're telling parts like the brain of the computer (the CPU) or its memory (RAM) to run at a higher speed than the company that made it originally set it to run. This can make games and programs run quicker, but just like a runner might get tired and hot, the computer parts get hotter and need extra cooling, like a bigger fan, to keep from getting damaged.

title: Why does China want to keep the yen weak in comparison to other countries?
text: China doesn't actually want to keep the yen weak; it's more focused on keeping its own currency, the yuan, stable and at a level that helps its own economy. Think of it like two kids trading toys: China wants to make sure the price tag on its own toys (exports like electronics and clothes) stays attractive so people around the world keep buying them. If the yen were to suddenly become very weak, it might make Japanese toys cheaper than China's, which could make things harder for Chinese factories. So, China watches the yen and other currencies carefully, but its main goal is to manage its own currency's value to help its businesses and keep its economy growing smoothly.

title: . Why are male contraceptives so basic?
text: Male contraceptives are basic because scientists have found it much harder to safely stop millions of sperm every day compared to stopping just one egg each month, and because there hasn't been as much money or research put into making new options for men as there has been for women.

title: What muscles are the least used and why do humans still have them?
text: Some muscles in our bodies are like old toys we don't play with much anymore, but we still keep them around. For example, the muscles that let some people wiggle their ears or move their scalp are leftovers from our animal ancestors, who used them to swivel their ears to hear danger better. We don't really need them now, but they haven't completely disappeared because they don't cause any harm by sticking around.

title: Why do we remember insults more than compliments?
text: Imagine your brain is like a guard dog that's always watching out for danger—insults feel like a little attack or a threat, so your brain barks really loud and remembers that person and what they said to protect you next time, while compliments feel like a nice pat on the head that makes you happy for a moment but don't need to be remembered for safety.

title: There was a scene which Charlie Chaplin was in a cage with the lion. Is it a real scene? How comes the lion was so harmless?
text: Yes, that's a real scene from Charlie Chaplin's 1928 silent movie "The Circus," and the lion was actually harmless because it was very old, tired, and had its teeth and claws removed to keep everyone safe during filming.

title: Why, when our ears pop, does it seem like we suddenly have HD hearing?
text: When your ears pop, it's like opening a tiny door that was stuck shut inside your ear—that door is actually a tube that connects your ear to the back of your nose, and it helps keep the air pressure the same on both sides of your eardrum. Sometimes, like when you're in an airplane or driving up a mountain, the air pressure changes and that tube closes, making everything sound muffled. When your ears pop, the tube opens back up, letting the pressure balance out and suddenly your eardrum can vibrate just right again, so sounds become clear and sharp, almost like switching from a fuzzy old radio to a crisp, high-definition speaker.

title: Why do companies care how their stocks are performing since they already got the money in IPO?
text: Think of a company like a big piggy bank that sold some of its shiny coins (stocks) to people during an IPO to get money for new toys or tools. Even after that sale, the company cares about how much people think those coins are worth because if the price goes up, it’s like everyone saying the piggy bank is really great—this makes it easier for the company to sell more coins later if it needs more money, and it makes the people who work there (who often get coins as rewards) happy and rich too!

title: why is C-4 or plastic explosives so powerful for being so small?
text: Think of C-4 like a super angry crowd of tiny people all packed together. Normally they're just standing still, but if you give them a little push (with a detonator), they all try to run out of the way at the exact same second and super, super fast.
